A hash map stores each key-value pair at an index produced by a hash function. When two keys hash to the same index, the map has a collision.

Most hash maps resolve collisions by chaining. Each bucket holds a linked list or tree of entries that share that index. A lookup hashes the key, walks the bucket, and compares keys until it finds a match.

Open addressing resolves collisions by probing for the next empty slot. Linear probing checks the next index; quadratic probing jumps by increasing squares; double hashing uses a second hash function to set the step size.

Chaining keeps the table simple but uses extra memory for pointers. Open addressing saves memory but suffers from clustering, where collisions form dense blocks and slow lookups.

A good hash function spreads keys uniformly and keeps collisions rare. A bad one maps many keys to the same bucket and turns the map into a slow list.

A database index is a separate data structure, usually a B-tree, that maps column values to the locations of rows in a table.

When a query filters on an indexed column, the database searches the index first. It finds the matching value, follows the pointer to the row, and reads only the needed data. Without an index, the database scans every row.

Indexes speed up lookups, joins, and sorting on the indexed columns. They also slow down writes, because every insert, update, or delete must update the index too. They consume disk space and memory.

An index hurts when it is unused. The database still pays to maintain it on writes, but the query planner never chooses it. This happens when the column has low cardinality, such as a boolean flag, where most rows match. It happens when a query filters with a function on the column, like `UPPER(email)`, because the index stores the raw value, not the transformed one. It happens when the leading columns of a composite index are skipped.

An index also hurts when it is too narrow. If a query needs columns not in the index, the database must look up each matching row in the main table. This back-and-forth, called a key lookup, can cost more than a full scan.

A covering index, which includes every column the query needs, avoids the lookup. But it is wider, costs more to maintain, and may not fit in memory.

The right index matches the queries that run often and the predicates that select few rows. The wrong index is overhead with no benefit.

A good hash function spreads keys uniformly and keeps collisions rare. A bad one maps many keys to the same bucket and turns the map into a slow list.

A mutex protects a program against race conditions on shared data.

A race condition happens when two threads read and write the same memory at overlapping times. Thread A reads a counter, thread B reads the same counter, both add one, and both write back the old result plus one. The counter increments once instead of twice.

A mutex is a lock. One thread acquires it before touching the shared data. The operating system or runtime lets only one thread hold the lock at a time. Other threads that want the lock wait until the holder releases it.

With the mutex, the two increments run one after the other. Each thread reads the current value, adds one, and writes the new value back before the next thread starts. The counter ends up correct.

A mutex does not protect against every concurrency problem. It does not prevent deadlocks, where two threads each hold a lock the other wants. It does not stop a thread from accessing the data without taking the lock. It only serializes access for threads that use it correctly.

I need to explain garbage collection in plain, factual prose with named subjects and concrete nouns. No preamble, no summary, no meta-narration.

A garbage collector finds memory that the running program can no longer reach.

The program keeps a set of starting points called roots. These are global variables, local variables on active call stacks, CPU registers, and any handles the runtime itself holds. The collector treats every object these roots point to as alive.

From each root, the collector follows every pointer field inside every live object. It marks each object it visits. If an object is already marked, the collector skips it and moves on. This walk covers the whole reachable graph.

Any object on the heap that never got a mark is unreachable. The program has no path to it through variables, fields, or registers. The collector reclaims that memory.

Some collectors, like those using reference counting, track the number of pointers to each object instead. When the count drops to zero, the object is unreachable and the collector frees it immediately. Reference counting misses cycles: object A points to object B, B points back to A, and nothing else points to either. Their counts stay above zero, so a separate cycle detector or a tracing pass must clean them up.

Tracing collectors pause the program while they walk the graph, or they run concurrently and track changes the program makes during the walk. Generational collectors split objects by age. Most objects die young, so the collector scans the young generation often and the old generation rarely.

The collector does not know what the program will need next. It only knows what the program can still reach.

A race condition is a bug that appears when two threads touch the same data at the same time and the outcome depends on which thread finishes first.

Picture two clerks updating a shared ledger. The ledger shows a balance of 100. Clerk A reads 100, adds 50, and intends to write 150. Clerk B reads 100 at the same moment, subtracts 30, and intends to write 70. Clerk A writes 150. Then Clerk B writes 70. The final balance is 70, not 120. One update vanished.

The program did not miscompute the arithmetic. Each clerk computed correctly from the value they saw. The failure was in the timing: the second write stomped on the first because neither clerk knew the other was editing the same line.

A race condition needs three things: shared memory, at least one thread writing to it, and no ordering that forces the writes to happen one at a time. Reads alone cannot race; two reads of the same value always produce the same result. A write paired with another write, or a write paired with a read, creates the hazard.

Programmers prevent race conditions with locks, atomic operations, or by giving each thread its own copy of the data. The right fix depends on how often the threads share the data and how much performance matters.

A CPU cache speeds a program by keeping recently used memory close to the processor.

Main memory sits far from the CPU on a separate chip, and a trip there takes hundreds of clock cycles. The cache is a smaller, faster memory bank inside or beside the processor. When the CPU reads a byte, it fetches a whole block of neighboring bytes into the cache. Programs tend to reuse the same variables and walk arrays in order, so the next access often hits the cache instead of main memory.

A cache hit reads in a few cycles. A cache miss stalls the CPU while it waits for main memory. The cache therefore rewards patterns that stay in one place: loops over small arrays, repeated function calls, and compact data structures. It punishes scattered access, such as chasing pointers through a linked list, because each jump likely misses and fetches a new block.

Caches are arranged in levels. L1 is smallest and fastest, often 32 to 64 kilobytes per core. L2 is larger and slower. L3 is shared across cores and slower still. Data that fits in L1 runs close to the CPU's native speed; data that spills to main memory runs at memory speed.

The cache also exploits temporal locality and spatial locality. Temporal locality means an address used once is likely to be used again soon. Spatial locality means an address near a recently used address is likely to be used next. The hardware guesses both and prefetches blocks accordingly.

A programmer can help the cache by keeping hot data small and contiguous, by accessing memory in predictable strides, and by avoiding false sharing, where two threads write different variables that happen to live in the same cache block and force constant invalidation between cores.

An HTTP request is idempotent when making it once and making it many times produce the same result on the server.

A `GET` request is idempotent because it only reads. Calling it again returns the same resource and changes nothing. A `PUT` that replaces a user's name with "Lee" is idempotent: the first call sets the name to "Lee", and repeated calls leave it as "Lee". A `POST` that creates a new order is not idempotent: each call adds another order.

Idempotency matters when networks fail. A client sends a request, the connection drops, and the client cannot tell whether the server received it. If the request is idempotent, the client can retry safely. If it is not, a retry might charge a card twice or ship a second package.

The HTTP specification lists methods by idempotency. `GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and `OPTIONS` are idempotent. `POST` and `PATCH` are not, though a carefully written `PATCH` can be.

Idempotency does not mean the response is identical each time. A `DELETE` returns `200` the first time and `404` later; the resource is still gone. The server state is what must stay the same.

APIs often add idempotency keys for non-idempotent operations. The client sends a unique key with a `POST`; the server stores the key and ignores duplicate requests that carry it. This makes a risky retry safe without changing the method's nature.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a chain of name servers.

A browser or program starts with a resolver, usually run by the operating system or the local network. The resolver checks its cache first. If the name is there, it returns the address immediately.

If the name is not cached, the resolver asks a root name server. The root server does not know the address, but it points the resolver to the server for the top-level domain, such as `.com` or `.org`.

The resolver asks that top-level server. It points the resolver to the authoritative server for the specific domain, such as `example.com`.

The resolver asks the authoritative server. That server holds the record that maps the name to an IP address. It returns the address, and the resolver passes it back to the program.

Each answer comes with a time-to-live value. The resolver caches the record for that many seconds and reuses it for later requests. When the time expires, the resolver asks again.

If a name has multiple addresses, the server can return them all. The resolver or the application picks one, often in round-robin order.

A deadlock is a standoff between threads that each hold a resource the other needs.

Thread A locks the account table. Thread B locks the transaction log. Thread A then asks for the transaction log and waits because Thread B holds it. Thread B asks for the account table and waits because Thread A holds it. Neither releases what it has. Neither gets what it wants. Both wait forever.

One way to avoid this is to make every thread acquire locks in the same order. If both threads always lock the account table before the transaction log, then Thread B cannot hold the transaction log while waiting for the account table, because it would have needed the account table first. The circular wait collapses into a queue.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket numbered by the key's hash code. Two keys can land in the same bucket; that is a collision.

Most hash maps resolve collisions by chaining or open addressing.

Chaining keeps a linked list or tree in each bucket. When a new key hashes to an occupied bucket, the map appends it to that list. Lookup scans the list and compares keys with `equals`. Java's `HashMap` uses a linked list and switches to a balanced tree when a bucket grows past eight entries.

Open addressing stores all entries in one array. When a slot is taken, the probe sequence checks the next slot—linear, quadratic, or double hashing—until it finds the key or an empty cell. Python's `dict` and Rust's `std::collections::HashMap` use variants of open addressing.

Load factor governs performance. As the ratio of entries to buckets rises, collisions cluster. The map resizes to a larger array and rehashes entries when the load factor crosses a threshold, often 0.75.

The hash function matters. A poor one maps many keys to the same bucket and turns the map into a slow list. A good one spreads keys uniformly across buckets.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. The receiver uses those numbers to reassemble the stream in the right order and to detect gaps.

Each segment carries a sequence number. The receiver acknowledges the next expected byte with an ACK. If a segment arrives out of order, the receiver holds it in a buffer until the missing bytes show up. The sender retransmits anything not acknowledged within the retransmission timeout, or after three duplicate ACKs trigger fast retransmit.

Flow control keeps the receiver from drowning. The window field in every ACK tells the sender how much buffer space remains. The sender stays within that limit.

Congestion control keeps the network from drowning. It starts slowly, probes for available capacity, and backs off when packets drop. Tahoe, Reno, and CUBIC differ mainly in how they detect loss and how fast they recover.

The result is a single, ordered byte stream across an unreliable network.

A mutex protects a program against race conditions on shared data.

A race condition happens when two threads read and write the same memory without ordering. Thread A reads a counter, adds one, and writes it back. Thread B does the same between A's read and write. One increment disappears.

A mutex is a lock. One thread acquires it before touching the shared data. The operating system lets only one thread hold the lock at a time. Other threads block until the holder releases it.

The protected region is called the critical section. It should be as small as possible: only the reads and writes that must be atomic. Holding a mutex while doing unrelated work slows other threads for no reason.

A mutex does not prevent deadlocks by itself. If thread 1 locks A then B, and thread 2 locks B then A, both can wait forever. The program must order its locks.

Mutexes also do not fix bugs in the data itself. They only serialize access. If the shared state is inconsistent when the lock is released, every thread sees the inconsistency.

Garbage collection finds unused memory by tracing reachable objects from a set of roots.

The roots are the starting points: local variables on thread stacks, static fields, and CPU registers that hold references. Anything the program can reach directly is alive.

The collector walks from each root to the objects it references, then to the objects those reference, and so on. Every object it touches is marked as reachable. Objects the walk never reaches are unreachable, and their memory can be reclaimed.

Some collectors add a reference count to each object. When the count drops to zero, the object is unreachable. Reference counting misses cycles: object A points to B, B points to A, and neither count reaches zero even though nothing else points to either. Tracing collectors catch cycles because neither A nor B is reachable from a root.

Generational collectors exploit a pattern: most objects die young. They divide the heap into generations and scan the young one often, since it produces most garbage. Objects that survive several collections move to an older generation, which the collector scans less frequently.

The collector must pause the program to keep object references from changing while it traces, or it must use incremental or concurrent techniques that track changes as the program runs. A full stop-the-world pause traces the entire heap in one go. Concurrent collectors trade some throughput and complexity for shorter pauses.

A race condition is a bug that appears when two or more threads or processes read and write shared data in an order the programmer did not intend.

Picture two clerks updating the same ledger. Each clerk reads the current balance, adds a deposit, and writes the new total back. Clerk A reads $100. Before A writes, clerk B reads the same $100. A writes $120. B writes $130. One deposit vanishes; the final balance is wrong, and neither clerk saw the other's work.

The root cause is the read-modify-write sequence. The operation is not atomic. The processor and the language do not guarantee that the three steps run as one unbroken unit unless the programmer uses a lock, an atomic instruction, or another synchronization mechanism.

Race conditions are not limited to counters. They corrupt linked lists when one thread inserts a node while another traverses it. They produce torn reads on 64-bit values on 32-bit systems. They cause a check-then-act pattern to fail when another thread changes the condition between the check and the act.

The bug is also timing-dependent. It may hide for days because the threads rarely interleave at the critical moment, then surface under load. That makes races hard to reproduce and dangerous to ignore.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping copies of recently used memory close to the processor.

Main memory sits far from the cores, on separate chips connected by a bus. A fetch from DRAM can take a hundred nanoseconds or more. The cache is a small, fast SRAM bank on the same die as the CPU. A hit there completes in a few cycles.

Programs tend to access the same data repeatedly, and nearby addresses in quick succession. Caches exploit this with two rules. Temporal locality means a byte used once is likely to be used again soon. Spatial locality means a byte used is likely to be near another byte used next. The cache stores whole lines, typically 64 bytes, so one fetch brings in the target and its neighbors.

Caches are arranged in levels. L1 is smallest and fastest, often split into one cache for instructions and one for data. L2 is larger and slower. L3 is larger still and shared across cores. The CPU checks L1 first, then L2, then L3, then main memory. Each miss costs more cycles.

When a core writes, the cache must keep copies consistent. Write-through updates memory immediately; write-back updates memory only when the line is evicted. Multicore systems use coherence protocols, such as MESI, so each core knows whether another core has modified a line.

A cache miss can erase the benefit. A program that jumps through memory randomly keeps missing. A program that walks arrays sequentially keeps hitting. The difference can be an order of magnitude.

I need to explain idempotency for an HTTP API in plain, factual prose.

An idempotent HTTP method produces the same server state when called once as when called many times. A client can send the same request twice without creating two effects.

`GET`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` are idempotent by design. `GET /orders/42` returns the same order whether the client calls it once or ten times. `PUT /orders/42` with a complete replacement body sets the resource to that state; repeating it leaves the resource unchanged. `DELETE /orders/42` removes the order; a second `DELETE` returns `404` because the order is already gone, but the server state stays the same.

`POST` is usually not idempotent. `POST /orders` creates a new order each time. A retry after a timeout can create a duplicate unless the client sends an idempotency key.

Idempotency matters for retries. Networks drop packets, servers time out, and clients cannot always tell whether a request reached the server. If the method is idempotent, the client can safely resend. If it is not, the client needs another safeguard.

An idempotency key is a token the client sends in a header, such as `Idempotency-Key: abc-123`. The server stores the key with the result of the first request and returns that result for repeats instead of re-running the operation. Stripe's API uses this pattern for `POST` requests that create charges.

Idempotency is about side effects, not response bodies. A `DELETE` may return `200` on the first call and `404` on the second; both leave the resource deleted. The state of the server is what must stay stable across repeated calls.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a hierarchy of servers, each one closer to the answer.

A browser or program starts with a stub resolver on the local machine. The stub resolver checks its cache. If the name is not there, it sends a query to a recursive resolver, usually run by the ISP, the company network, or a public service such as Google DNS at 8.8.8.8 or Cloudflare at 1.1.1.1.

The recursive resolver asks the root servers. Thirteen logical root servers, named A through M, know where the top-level domains live. The resolver asks a root server for `example.com`. The root server replies with the addresses of the `.com` name servers.

The resolver then asks a `.com` name server. That server knows where the `example.com` name servers are. It returns their addresses.

The resolver asks one of those `example.com` name servers. That server holds the record for `www.example.com`, or a record that points elsewhere. It returns the IP address.

The resolver gives the address back to the stub resolver, which gives it to the browser. The resolver also caches the answer, and every server along the way caches the records for the time specified in their TTL.

If a record is missing, the resolver returns an error. If a name points to another name through a CNAME, the resolver follows the chain until it reaches an A or AAAA record with an IP address.

A deadlock is a standoff between two or more threads, each holding a lock the others need.

Picture two clerks and two ledgers. Clerk A locks ledger 1, then asks for ledger 2. Clerk B already locked ledger 2 and now asks for ledger 1. Both wait. Neither releases. They stay stuck forever unless something outside breaks the tie.

The cause is a circular wait. Each thread holds one resource and requests another, and the chain loops back to the start. Deadlocks also need the other three conditions: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, and no preemption. Break any one, and the deadlock cannot form.

The cleanest fix is lock ordering. Every thread in the program acquires its locks in the same global order. If ledger 1 always comes before ledger 2, clerk B cannot lock ledger 2 first. The circular wait becomes impossible.

Other fixes work too. Lock timeout lets a thread back out and retry. One-lock-at-a-time removes hold-and-wait. Resource hierarchy assigns each lock a rank. But lock ordering is the usual choice because it is simple and removes the problem at the source.

Deadlocks do not show up in every run. They need the right interleaving, so tests often miss them. They appear under load, then freeze a service until someone restarts it.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket chosen by the key's hash code. When two keys land in the same bucket, the map has a collision.

Most hash maps resolve collisions by chaining: each bucket holds a linked list or tree of entries that share that bucket. The map hashes the key, finds the bucket, then walks the list and compares keys with `equals` until it finds the right one.

Open addressing handles collisions differently. It stores every entry inside the table array itself. When a bucket is full, the probe continues to the next slot—linear, quadratic, or by a second hash—until it finds an empty one. Retrieval follows the same probe sequence.

Load factor governs performance. Too many entries per bucket make chains long and lookups slow. A well-implemented map resizes the table and rehashes entries when the load crosses a threshold, usually around 0.75.

Java's `HashMap` uses chaining. Each bucket starts as a linked list; once a chain reaches length 8 and the table has at least 64 buckets, that chain becomes a red-black tree. This keeps worst-case lookup near O(log n) instead of O(n).

A database index is a separate data structure that points to rows in a table so the database can find them without reading every row.

Most indexes are B-trees. The database keeps the indexed column values sorted in a tree of pages on disk. To look up a value, it walks from the root page to a leaf page, then follows the pointer to the row. A lookup touches a few pages instead of scanning the whole table.

An index helps when the query filters, joins, or sorts on the indexed column. It also helps enforce uniqueness and foreign keys. Without an index, the database reads every row and compares it to the query condition.

An index hurts when it costs more to maintain than it saves. Every insert, update, or delete on the table must also update every index on that table. A table with six indexes does six extra write operations per row change. That slows writes and consumes disk I/O.

An index also hurts when the query would scan most of the table anyway. If a query returns 80% of the rows, the database may skip the index and scan the table because random index lookups are slower than a sequential scan.

Indexes consume disk space. They can bloat after many updates if the database does not reclaim dead entries promptly. They can also fragment, though the practical cost of fragmentation varies by database and workload.

Covering indexes help reads because the query gets all its columns from the index alone. But a covering index with many columns is wider, uses more space, and slows writes more.

Indexes on low-cardinality columns—like a boolean flag—often help little because the database still has to inspect many rows. The query planner may ignore such an index.

Too many indexes are a common cause of slow writes. The right number depends on the read-to-write ratio and which queries actually run.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. The sender assigns each byte a sequence number. The receiver uses that number to put the bytes back in order and to detect gaps.

When a segment arrives out of order, the receiver holds it in a buffer. It waits for the missing segment to fill the gap. Once the gap closes, TCP delivers the reordered stream to the application.

The receiver sends acknowledgments back. Each ACK names the next sequence number it expects. If the sender sees a gap in the ACKs, it retransmits the missing segment.

Duplicate ACKs trigger fast retransmit. If the sender gets three ACKs for the same sequence number, it resends that segment before the retransmission timer expires.

A retransmission timer covers lost segments. If the sender does not get an ACK in time, it sends the segment again. The timeout adjusts to measured round-trip times.

Flow control keeps the receiver from being overrun. The receiver advertises a window size that limits how much data the sender can have in flight. Congestion control, separate from ordering, limits how much data enters the network.

A mutex protects a program against the wrong result when two threads touch the same data at once.

A thread locks the mutex before it enters a critical section. While the lock is held, any other thread that tries to lock the same mutex waits. The first thread finishes, unlocks the mutex, and the waiting thread proceeds. Only one thread runs the protected code at a time.

Without a mutex, two threads can read, modify, and write the same value in overlapping steps. One increment can overwrite another. A check-then-act sequence can run twice. A half-written structure can be read by another thread.

A mutex does not prevent deadlocks by itself. Thread A can lock mutex 1 and wait for mutex 2 while thread B holds mutex 2 and waits for mutex 1. The programmer orders the locks, or uses a single lock, to avoid that.

A mutex also does not make a shared value atomic. It only keeps threads from entering the guarded region together. The data inside still needs correct invariants.

Mutexes are coarse. Locking a big structure for every access serializes work that could run in parallel. Finer locks help concurrency but raise the chance of deadlock or inconsistency if the boundaries are wrong.

A garbage collector finds unused memory by tracing reachable objects from a set of roots.

The roots are the starting points: local variables on thread stacks, static fields, and CPU registers that hold references. The collector treats every object these roots point to as alive. It then follows every reference inside those objects to more objects, and so on, until it has marked every reachable object.

Any object the trace never reaches is unused. The collector sweeps those objects and reclaims their memory.

Reference counting is a different approach. Each object stores a count of incoming references. When a reference disappears, the count drops. When the count hits zero, the object is unused and the collector frees it immediately. Reference counting cannot reclaim cycles: two objects that point only to each other keep each other’s counts above zero even when nothing else references them.

Generational collectors exploit a fact: most objects die young. They divide the heap into generations and trace the young generation more often. Objects that survive several collections move to an older generation, which the collector scans less frequently.

A tracing collector pauses the program while it walks the heap. The length of that pause depends on the number of live objects, not the heap size. Concurrent and incremental collectors interleave tracing with program execution to shorten or eliminate the pause, at the cost of more total work and higher complexity.

A race condition happens when a program's result depends on the timing or order of events that the programmer does not control.

Consider two threads that increment the same counter. Each thread reads the counter, adds one, and writes it back. Thread A reads 5. Before A writes 6, thread B reads 5. B writes 6. A writes 6. The counter ends at 6, though two increments ran.

The bug is not that the threads ran at the same moment; it is that their read-modify-write steps interleaved. The final value depends on which thread won each race.

Race conditions also appear in check-then-act sequences. One thread checks that a file does not exist, then creates it. Another thread does the same check between the first thread's check and its creation. Both threads create the file, or one overwrites the other.

They appear in event-driven code too. A handler reads a UI field, then acts on it. A second event updates the field between the read and the act. The handler uses stale data.

The fix is to make the sequence atomic: a mutex, a lock, an atomic compare-and-swap, or a single database statement that checks and updates together. The right tool depends on what must not interleave.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping copies of recently used memory close to the processor.

Main memory sits far from the CPU, measured in nanoseconds to reach. A cache sits on the same chip or nearby, and the CPU can read it in a fraction of that time. When the CPU needs data, it checks the cache first. If the data is there, it avoids the slower trip to RAM.

Programs tend to reuse data they just touched. They also tend to access nearby memory together. The cache exploits both habits. It loads a whole block of memory around each requested address, so later reads to neighboring addresses hit the cache.

Caches are arranged in levels. L1 is smallest and fastest, often a few kilobytes per core. L2 is larger and slower. L3 is larger still and shared across cores. A hit in L1 costs a couple of cycles. A miss that reaches main memory can cost hundreds.

A cache miss stalls the CPU. The processor must wait while the cache line travels up from memory. Programs that jump around memory cause many misses. Programs that walk arrays sequentially cause fewer.

Writes work similarly. The CPU can write to cache and defer updating main memory. A write-back policy keeps modified cache lines until they must be flushed. A write-through policy updates memory immediately, which is slower but simpler.

Multicore caches add coherence work. If one core writes a value that another core has cached, the hardware must invalidate or update the other copy. False sharing happens when two cores write different variables that happen to live in the same cache line; the hardware treats them as the same data and bounces the line between cores.

A cache therefore helps most when the program reuses a small working set. It helps least when the program streams through more data than the cache can hold.

With `POST`, a retry risks a duplicate unless the server stores the idempotency key and returns the previous response.

A request can be idempotent yet still change server state. `DELETE` changes state. Idempotency does not mean "no side effects"; it means the side effects do not accumulate beyond the first application.

Safe methods are a related but narrower idea. `GET` and `HEAD` are safe because they should not change state at all. All safe methods are idempotent, but not all idempotent methods are safe.

A user types `example.com` into a browser. The browser asks a resolver to find the address.

The resolver first checks its cache. If it recently looked up `example.com`, it returns the stored address and stops.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket numbered by the key's hash code. When two keys land in the same bucket, the map has a collision.

Most hash maps chain colliding entries. Each bucket holds a linked list, array, or tree of entries that share that bucket. A lookup first computes the bucket index from the key's hash, then scans the entries in that bucket and compares keys with `equals` until it finds a match.

Java's `HashMap` uses linked lists by default and switches a bucket to a red-black tree when the list grows past eight entries. Python's `dict` uses open addressing instead: it probes a sequence of alternative slots inside the array until it finds the key or an empty slot.

A database index is a separate structure that points to rows so the database can find them without reading the whole table.

A secondary index stores the indexed value plus the primary key, so a query may need two tree walks.

They hurt on reads when the query returns many rows. If a query matches half the table, scanning the index and fetching rows one by one is slower than reading the table sequentially. The database's optimizer keeps a threshold—MySQL calls it the "range optimizer," PostgreSQL uses cost estimates—and may ignore the index.

They hurt when they are unused but maintained. An index on a column that is never filtered or joined consumes disk space, cache, and write bandwidth. In PostgreSQL, `pg_stat_user_indexes` shows how often an index is scanned; a zero count over a long interval is evidence the index is dead weight.

They hurt when they fragment. Repeated updates can split and scatter B-tree pages, making range scans less sequential and the tree deeper than it needs to be. Some databases need periodic `REINDEX` or `OPTIMIZE TABLE`.

They hurt when the query cannot use them. A `LIKE '%word'` pattern, a function wrapped around the column like `UPPER(email)`, or an implicit type conversion can prevent the database from using an otherwise useful index.

An index is a trade: faster selected reads for slower writes and more storage. The right index supports a real query pattern; the wrong one is a tax on every mutation.

A mutex protects a program against races on shared data when multiple threads run at once.

A race happens when two threads read and write the same memory without ordering. Thread A reads a counter, adds one, and writes it back. Thread B does the same. Without a mutex, both can read 5, both write 6, and the counter loses an increment.

A mutex solves this by letting only one thread enter a critical section at a time. Before touching the shared data, a thread locks the mutex. Other threads that try to lock it block until the owner unlocks it. The read-modify-write sequence becomes atomic from the other threads' view.

Most operating systems implement mutexes with a kernel object or a futex: fast when uncontended, slower when threads must sleep and wake.

A garbage collector finds unused memory by tracing what the program can still reach.

The collector starts from roots: local variables on thread stacks, global variables, and CPU registers that hold references. It marks every object those roots point to, then every object those objects point to, and so on. Any object not reached by this walk is unused.

Most collectors use a tri-color scheme. Objects start white. The collector marks reachable objects gray when it finds a reference, then black when it has scanned their fields. White objects remain when the trace ends; the collector reclaims them.

Reference counting is a different approach. Each object stores a count of incoming references. When a reference disappears, the count drops. When it hits zero, the object is unused and the collector frees it immediately. Reference counting cannot reclaim cycles: two objects that point only to each other keep each other's count above zero.

Generational collectors exploit a pattern observed in most programs: young objects die fast, old objects linger. They divide the heap into generations and trace the young generation often, the old generation rarely. A write barrier records when an old object gains a reference to a young one, so the collector does not miss live young objects.

Some collectors, like Go's, combine tracing with compaction. After marking live objects, they move those objects together and update every pointer. This eliminates fragmentation and keeps allocation fast.

The collector does not ask the program which objects are needed. It reconstructs need from the graph of references the program can still follow.

A race condition is a bug where a program's result depends on the timing or order of operations that run at the same time.

Consider two threads that increment the same counter. Each thread reads the counter, adds one, and writes it back. Thread A reads 5. Before A writes 6, Thread B reads 5. Both threads write 6. The counter should be 7, but it is 6. The final value depends on which read happened first.

The operations are not atomic. The read, add, and write are separate steps. The threads interleave between those steps, so the update is lost.

A mutex prevents this by making the read-add-write sequence run in one piece. Only one thread holds the lock at a time, so the second read cannot slip in before the first write finishes.

Race conditions also appear in file writes, message queues, and lazy initialization. Any shared state that two threads touch without synchronization is a candidate.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping recently used memory close to the core.

Programs access memory in bursts. A loop may read the same array element many times, or touch nearby cells in sequence. DRAM takes hundreds of cycles to return data. The cache stores copies of recently accessed DRAM locations in fast SRAM right next to the core. A hit returns in a few cycles; a miss pays the full DRAM latency.

Caches exploit two patterns. Temporal locality means an address used once is likely to be used again soon. Spatial locality means an address near a recently used one is likely next. A cache line, typically 64 bytes, fetches a whole block on the first miss so later nearby accesses hit.

Hardware prefetchers spot striding access patterns and fetch the next lines before the program asks. The compiler and programmer can also lay out data so hot fields sit together and fit in fewer cache lines.

A cache hurts when the working set exceeds its size. Thrashing occurs when frequently used blocks evict each other before reuse. False sharing happens when two cores write different variables that share a cache line, forcing constant invalidation traffic between cores.

A cache does not make DRAM faster. It makes the average access cheaper by keeping the right data nearby.

The whole exchange usually takes milliseconds and hides behind a single call to `getaddrinfo` or a browser's address bar.

A deadlock is a standoff between threads or processes that are each waiting for something another one holds.

Thread B would try for the file, find A holding it, and wait there without holding the row. A finishes and releases both; B then proceeds.

Lock ordering works only when the set of resources and a global order are known. It does not help with locks acquired dynamically or across independent modules.

A mutex protects against interleaving, not against logic errors inside the critical section. If the code inside the lock is wrong, the bug still runs, just alone.

Generational collectors exploit a fact: most objects die young. They divide the heap into generations and scan the young generation often, since most garbage collects there. Objects that survive several collections move to an older generation, which the collector scans less frequently.

The pause comes from the mark phase. While the collector traces references, the program must not move the graph underneath it. Stop-the-world collectors pause all threads. Concurrent collectors trace while the program runs, but they need a final pass to catch references the program changed during tracing.

The collector does not know what the program "meant" to keep. It only knows what the program can still touch.

The program lost an update not because either clerk was wrong alone, but because their reads and writes interleaved. A mutex, used correctly, prevents this by letting only one clerk hold the ledger at a time.

When the CPU reads an address, the hardware first checks the cache. If the data is there, the CPU gets it in a few cycles instead of waiting for DRAM.

Caches exploit two patterns in real programs. Temporal locality means a program tends to reuse data it just touched. Spatial locality means a program tends to touch nearby addresses soon after one another. The cache therefore stores whole blocks, called cache lines, typically 64 bytes, so one fetch covers several likely future accesses.

A cache hit reads from the fast cache. A cache miss falls back to main memory and stalls the pipeline. Programs that walk arrays sequentially get many hits; programs that jump through pointers or large structures get many misses.

Modern CPUs use multiple cache levels. L1 is smallest and fastest, often split into instruction and data caches. L2 and L3 are larger and slower but still faster than RAM. A hit in L3 beats a trip to DRAM.

The cache also writes. A write-back cache updates only the cache line at first and flushes to main memory later. A write-through cache updates both at once. The choice trades consistency for speed.

Good cache performance comes from data layout and access order, not from clock speed alone. A program that keeps its working set small and sequential can run many times faster than one that scatters its memory accesses across a large footprint.

Idempotency means the API gives the same result whether the client sends a request once or many times.

A safe idempotent method is GET. Calling GET on `/orders/42` ten times returns the same order each time, assuming no other request changes it. The server does not alter state.

POST is usually not idempotent. Two POSTs to `/orders` create two orders. The server changes state on every call.

PUT and DELETE are meant to be idempotent. Sending PUT `/orders/42` with the same body twice leaves the order in the same state as sending it once. Sending DELETE `/orders/42` twice leaves the order deleted; the second call returns a 404, but the resource state matches the first call.

This matters for retries. Networks drop packets and clients time out. A client that retries an idempotent request does not risk double-charging a customer or double-shipping a package. The server can safely process the retry because the outcome is the same.

Idempotency keys are one way to make POST idempotent. The client sends a unique key with the first request and includes the same key on retries. The server stores the key and returns the stored response instead of running the operation again.

The guarantee is about effect, not about the exact HTTP response code. A second DELETE may return 404 when the first returned 200, yet the operation is still idempotent because the resource stays deleted.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a chain of name servers.

When a program needs `example.com`, it first asks a recursive resolver. The resolver checks its cache. If it has no answer, it starts at the root.

The root servers know only the next authority. They point the resolver to the servers for `.com`. The `.com` servers point to the name servers for `example.com`. Those name servers return the A record, which holds the IPv4 address, or the AAAA record for IPv6.

Each step uses a UDP query on port 53. The resolver follows referrals until it gets a final answer, then returns it to the program.

Caching shortens later lookups. Every record carries a time-to-live, in seconds. The resolver keeps the answer that long and reuses it. When the TTL expires, the resolver asks again.

If a name maps to multiple addresses, the resolver may return them all. The client usually tries the first one. DNS itself does not pick the closest server; that is the job of routing and anycast.

A deadlock is a standoff between two or more threads, each holding a lock the others need.

Thread A locks the account table and waits for the inventory table. Thread B locks the inventory table and waits for the account table. Neither releases. Neither proceeds. Both sit forever unless something outside breaks the tie.

One way to avoid it is to lock resources in a fixed order. Every thread that needs both tables takes the account table first, then the inventory table. A thread that already holds inventory and needs account must release inventory, take account, then retake inventory. The circular wait disappears because all threads agree on the same direction.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket numbered by the key's hash code. When two keys land in the same bucket, that is a collision.

Most hash maps resolve collisions by chaining. Each bucket holds a linked list or tree of entries. A lookup hashes the key, walks that bucket's chain, and compares keys until it finds a match.

Open addressing is the other common method. It stores every entry directly in the table array. When a bucket is full, the map probes forward—linearly, quadratically, or by a second hash—until it finds an empty slot. Lookup follows the same probe sequence.

Load factor governs performance. Chaining slows as buckets grow long; open addressing slows as clusters form. A hash map typically resizes and rehashes all entries into a larger array once the load factor crosses a threshold, often around 0.75.

Java's `HashMap` uses chaining and converts long chains into balanced trees. Python's `dict` uses open addressing with a probe sequence derived from the hash. The choice trades memory against worst-case lookup time.

A database index is a separate data structure that points to rows in a table, built on one or more columns so the database can find values without scanning every row.

Most indexes are B-trees. They keep keys sorted, so lookups, range scans, and ordered reads take O(log n) page accesses instead of O(n) row checks.

An index helps when the query filters, joins, or orders on the indexed columns. It also helps enforce uniqueness and foreign-key constraints.

An index hurts when its cost exceeds its benefit. Writes must update every index on the table, so each extra index slows inserts, updates, and deletes. Indexes consume disk space and memory. The optimizer may choose a bad plan and scan the index when a table scan would be faster. Low-cardinality columns, like a boolean flag, rarely help because the index returns too many rows. Covering indexes can speed reads but add write overhead. Fragmentation and stale statistics degrade performance over time.

In short: an index is a sorted shortcut to rows. It is worth building when queries repeatedly pay for the search it replaces, and costly when writes and maintenance outrun those savings.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. The sender assigns each byte a sequence number before it leaves the machine.

The receiver checks those numbers. If a segment arrives out of order, the receiver holds it in a buffer and sends an acknowledgment for the last contiguous byte it has received.

The sender keeps a window of unacknowledged bytes. When an acknowledgment comes back, it slides the window forward. Missing acknowledgments trigger a retransmission.

This sequence-number-and-acknowledgment loop restores order at the destination without requiring the network itself to deliver packets in order.

A mutex protects a program against race conditions on shared data.

A race condition happens when two threads read and write the same memory at the same time. One thread may overwrite another's change, or both may read a stale value and then write back a corrupted result.

A mutex is a lock. One thread acquires it before entering a critical section. While that thread holds the lock, any other thread that tries to acquire the same mutex blocks until the lock is released. This serializes access to the shared resource.

The mutex does not protect the data by itself. The programmer must acquire the mutex before every read or write of the shared state and release it after. If a thread touches the data without holding the lock, the race condition returns.

A mutex also prevents torn reads and writes on data larger than a single atomic word. It can coordinate ordering: a thread can wait for another thread to finish an update before it proceeds.

The cost is contention. If many threads fight for the same mutex, they spend time blocked instead of working. Deadlock occurs when two threads each hold one mutex and wait for the other's. Priority inversion can make a high-priority thread wait for a low-priority thread that holds the lock.

Garbage collection finds unused memory by tracing reachable objects from a set of roots.

The roots are the starting points the runtime already knows about: local variables on thread stacks, global variables, CPU registers, and handles held by the language runtime. Any object the program can still use must be reachable from at least one root.

The collector walks outward from these roots. It marks each object it reaches. If object A references object B, the collector marks B too. It follows references through fields, array slots, closures, and any other place the language stores pointers.

Objects the collector never marks are unreachable. The program has no path to them through any root. The collector treats them as garbage and reclaims their memory.

Most collectors use one of two strategies. Tracing collectors, such as mark-sweep and mark-compact, start from roots and mark live objects. Reference-counting collectors instead count incoming pointers to each object and reclaim objects whose count drops to zero. Reference counting misses cycles—two objects that point only to each other—so systems that use it add a cycle detector or a fallback trace.

Generational collectors exploit a common pattern: most objects die young. They divide the heap into generations, scan the young generation often, and scan the old generation only when necessary. This reduces pause time because young collections touch far fewer objects.

A collector may pause all threads to trace the heap, or it may run concurrently while the program mutates objects. Concurrent collectors must be careful: a mutator can change a reference after the collector has visited an object, hiding a live object from the trace. They use write barriers to catch changed references and keep the mark set correct.

The hard part is not finding garbage. It is finding it without stopping the program for too long, without using extra memory the program needs, and without moving objects the program still expects to stay put.

A race condition is a bug that appears when two threads touch the same data at the same time and the outcome depends on which thread wins.

Picture two clerks updating the same ledger. Each reads the balance, adds a deposit, and writes the new total. Clerk A reads $100. Clerk B reads $100 before A writes back. A writes $120. B writes $130, using the stale $100 as the base. The $20 deposit from A disappears.

The program did not crash. Both writes succeeded. The result is simply wrong because the second write ignored the first.

Race conditions hide because they usually pass. Most of the time the threads do not interleave in the losing order. They surface only under load, on slower machines, or after unrelated code changes shift the timing.

The fix is to make the read-add-write sequence atomic. A mutex, an atomic increment, or a compare-and-swap loop forces the second thread to wait until the first thread finishes, so no clerk ever writes from a stale balance.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping recently used memory close to the processor.

Main memory sits far from the CPU, and a trip there takes hundreds of clock cycles. The cache is smaller and faster, made of SRAM, and sits on or near the core. When the CPU reads an address, the hardware first checks the cache. A hit returns the data in a few cycles. A miss fetches a whole cache line—usually 64 bytes—from memory and stores it nearby.

Programs tend to reuse data they just touched, and they often access nearby addresses next. The cache exploits both habits. Temporal locality means a second read to the same spot finds it still loaded. Spatial locality means fetching a line brings in neighbors that the program probably wants soon.

A modern CPU has multiple levels. L1 is the smallest and fastest, often split into instruction and data caches. L2 is larger and slightly slower. L3 is shared across cores and slower still. Data moves up the hierarchy in cache lines and gets evicted when the set fills.

The speedup is real but fragile. A loop that strides through a large array with a step larger than a line wastes fetches. False sharing makes two cores repeatedly invalidate the same line. A cache miss on a hot path can stall the pipeline.

A cache does not change the program's result. It changes the cost of memory access, and most programs spend much of their time waiting on memory.

Idempotency means the same HTTP request can run more than once without changing the result beyond the first time.

A client sends a `PUT` to set a user's email. The network blinks. The client never sees the response, so it retries. A server that treats `PUT` as idempotent applies the change once and returns the same state on the second try. The email ends up set, not set twice.

`GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` are usually idempotent. `POST` usually is not: each `POST` to create an order makes a new order. `PATCH` depends on the operation. A patch that says "set status to shipped" is idempotent. A patch that says "add $10 to balance" is not.

The practical value is recovery. Networks drop replies, clients retry, and middleware may replay requests. An idempotent endpoint absorbs those repeats without duplicate charges, duplicate records, or duplicate side effects.

Idempotency is about the server's state, not the response body. The first request may return `201 Created`; the retry may return `200 OK`. Both leave the resource in the same shape.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a chain of name servers.

A browser or program sends the name, such as `example.com`, to a resolver. The resolver first checks its cache. If it has a recent answer, it returns the address immediately.

If the cache misses, the resolver asks a root server. The root server does not know the address, but it points the resolver to the server for the top-level domain, such as `.com`.

The resolver asks the `.com` server. That server points to the authoritative server for `example.com`.

The resolver asks the authoritative server. That server holds the record that maps `example.com` to an IP address. It returns the address.

The resolver caches the answer and hands it back to the browser. The browser then opens a connection to that IP address.

Each step uses a UDP query on port 53, though large replies fall back to TCP. Caching at every layer keeps the system from hammering the root servers and speeds up repeat lookups.

A deadlock is a standoff between threads. Each holds a resource the other needs, and neither can move.

Thread A locks the account table. Thread B locks the transaction log. A then asks for the log. B then asks for the account table. Both wait forever.

The cause is a circular wait. A waits for B. B waits for A. No thread releases its lock because each is stuck waiting.

One fix is lock ordering. Every thread must acquire locks in the same global order: account table first, then transaction log. If B already holds the transaction log and needs the account table, it must release the log, take the account table, then retake the log. The circle breaks because no thread can hold a later lock while waiting for an earlier one.

Deadlocks still hide when code paths are many and the lock order is not written down.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket numbered by the key's hash code. When two keys land in the same bucket, that is a collision.

Most hash maps resolve collisions by chaining. Each bucket holds a linked list or tree of entries that share that bucket. A lookup hashes the key, walks the list at that bucket, and compares keys until it finds a match.

Open addressing is the other common method. It places the entry in the next empty slot, using a probe sequence such as linear probing, quadratic probing, or double hashing. A lookup follows the same probe sequence.

Load factor governs performance. As the map fills, collisions rise and chains lengthen. Java's `HashMap` rehashes when the load factor exceeds 0.75. Python's dict resizes when two-thirds full.

A poor hash function makes collisions common even with few entries. A good hash function spreads keys uniformly across buckets. Cryptographic hash functions are overkill here; speed and distribution matter more.

Some maps switch from linked lists to balanced trees when a bucket grows too long. Java's `HashMap` does this at a chain length of eight, reducing worst-case lookup from O(n) to O(log n).

A database index is a separate data structure that points to rows in a table, built on one or more columns so the database can find values without scanning every row.

The most common index is a B-tree. It keeps column values sorted in a balanced tree of pages, so a lookup, range query, or ordered read can descend from root to leaf in O(log n) page reads instead of reading the whole table.

An index helps when the query filters, joins, or orders on the indexed column. It helps most when the selectivity is high: the query narrows the result to a small fraction of rows. It also helps enforce uniqueness and speed foreign-key lookups.

An index hurts when it is unused but must be maintained. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` on the table must update every index on that table. On a write-heavy table with many indexes, that maintenance cost dominates.

An index hurts when it is too wide. If a query returns many columns and the index does not cover them, the database looks up each matching row in the heap. This bookmark lookup can be slower than a full table scan, especially when the query returns a large share of rows.

An index hurts when it causes bad plan choices. A missing or misleading statistic can push the optimizer toward an index seek that reads many pages, or away from a better scan. Composite indexes hurt when the query does not use the leading columns, leaving the index unread.

An index hurts when it consumes space and memory. Each index stores a copy of part of the data; large indexes compete for buffer pool space and slow backups.

So an index is a trade-off: faster reads on specific columns, slower writes, more storage, and a new way for the optimizer to make a mistake. Add one when a measured query is slow and the access pattern is stable; avoid adding indexes speculatively.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. The sender assigns each byte a sequence number. The receiver acknowledges the highest contiguous sequence number it has received. Gaps trigger duplicate acknowledgments, and the sender retransmits the missing segment. The receiver buffers out-of-order segments and delivers bytes to the application only once the missing piece arrives.

A mutex protects shared data from races when multiple threads or processes touch it at once.

A race happens when two execution contexts read and write the same memory without ordering. One context may overwrite another's update, read a half-written structure, or see a torn value. A mutex prevents this by allowing only one context to enter a critical section at a time.

The mutex itself is a synchronization primitive with two states: locked and unlocked. A thread locks the mutex before entering the critical section. If another thread tries to lock the same mutex, it blocks until the owner unlocks it. This serializes access to the protected resource.

A mutex does not protect against every concurrency problem. It does not prevent deadlocks if threads acquire multiple mutexes in inconsistent orders. It does not prevent priority inversion, where a low-priority thread holds a lock a high-priority thread needs. It does not stop two threads from corrupting data if they both hold the lock but one writes invalid state.

Mutexes work best around small, well-defined critical sections. The protected region should be short and should touch only the shared state the mutex guards. Holding a mutex across I/O, sleep, or unrelated computation stalls other threads and wastes the serialization the mutex provides.

Common implementations include pthreads mutexes, Windows critical sections, std::mutex in C++, and threading.Lock in Python. Most offer variants such as recursive mutexes, which allow the same thread to relock, and read-write locks, which allow many readers or one writer.

Garbage collection finds unused memory by tracing reachable objects from a set of roots.

The roots are the starting points the collector already knows are alive: global variables, local variables on thread stacks, CPU registers, and handles held by the runtime. The collector walks references outward from these roots, marking every object it reaches.

An object the walk never reaches is unreachable from the running program. The collector treats it as garbage and reclaims its memory. This is tracing collection, used by Java's G1, .NET's GC, and Go's concurrent collector.

Some collectors add a second phase. After marking live objects, they sweep the heap and return unmarked blocks to free lists. Mark-sweep collectors do this. Mark-compact collectors move live objects together instead, eliminating fragmentation but pausing threads while objects move.

Reference counting is a different approach. Each object stores a count of incoming references. When a reference disappears, the count drops. When it hits zero, the object is reclaimed immediately. Python and Swift use this, often with a cycle detector because reference counts alone cannot collect circular references.

Generational collectors exploit a observed pattern: most objects die young. They divide the heap into generations, scan the young generation frequently, and promote survivors to older generations that are scanned less often. This reduces pause times because young collections touch less memory.

A collector may pause all application threads to do its work, as stop-the-world collectors do, or it may run concurrently with the program, as Java's ZGC and Go's GC attempt. Concurrent collection reduces pauses but adds complexity: the program can mutate references while the collector is tracing, so the collector needs barriers to catch changes.

A race condition is a bug that appears when two or more threads or processes read and write the same shared state at the same time, and the final result depends on which one finishes first.

Consider two threads that each add ten dollars to the same bank balance. The balance starts at zero. Each thread reads the balance, adds ten, and writes the result back. Thread A reads zero and computes ten. Before A writes, thread B reads zero and computes ten. Both write ten. The balance ends at ten instead of twenty. The order of execution changed the outcome.

The problem is the read-modify-write sequence. It is not atomic. The operating system can switch between threads after the read and before the write, so each thread acts on stale data.

Race conditions are not limited to memory. They can affect files, database rows, network sockets, or any resource that multiple actors touch without coordination.

The fix is to make the critical section atomic. A mutex, a lock, or an atomic compare-and-swap operation forces the threads to take turns. With a mutex, thread A reads, adds, and writes before thread B can enter. The balance ends at twenty.

Race conditions are hard to test because they depend on timing. A program can pass a thousand tests and fail in production when the scheduler pauses a thread at exactly the wrong moment.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping recently used memory close to the processor.

Main memory sits far from the cores, on separate chips connected by a bus. A fetch from DRAM can take a hundred nanoseconds or more. The cache is smaller SRAM on the same die as the core; an L1 hit takes a few clock cycles.

Programs reuse data. They read the same variable twice, or walk an array in order. The cache stores whole lines, typically 64 bytes, so one fetch pulls in nearby bytes. Sequential access often hits the cache repeatedly.

Caches are hierarchical. A modern x86 or ARM core has private L1 instruction and data caches, a private L2, and a shared L3. L1 is fastest and smallest; L3 is larger and slower but still faster than DRAM.

When the CPU needs a byte, it checks L1, then L2, then L3, then main memory. A hit in a closer cache avoids the slower trip outward. A miss stalls the pipeline until the data arrives.

The cache also exploits temporal locality: data used once is likely to be used again soon. It exploits spatial locality: data near a recently used address is likely to be used next. Good cache performance comes from matching the program's access pattern to these habits.

Idempotency means the same HTTP request can run more than once without changing the result beyond the first time.

A `GET` request is idempotent by nature. Calling it once or five times returns the same resource and leaves the server state unchanged.

A `PUT` request to `/users/123` with a fixed payload is idempotent. Sending it twice sets the user to the same values both times. The second request does not create a duplicate or accumulate changes.

A `POST` request to `/orders` is usually not idempotent. Sending it twice creates two orders. That is why payment endpoints often use idempotency keys: the client sends a unique key, and the server stores it so a retry with the same key does not charge the card again.

Idempotency matters because networks fail. A client may not receive the response and send the request again. If the request is idempotent, the retry is safe. If it is not, the retry may double-charge, double-book, or duplicate a record.

HTTP defines `GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and `OPTIONS` as idempotent by specification. `POST` and `PATCH` are not, though a careful implementation can make a specific `PATCH` idempotent if it assigns absolute values rather than applying deltas.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a chain of name servers.

A computer starts with a hostname, such as `example.com`. It first checks its own cache. If the name is not there, it asks a recursive resolver, usually run by the operating system, the ISP, or a public service such as Google DNS or Cloudflare.

The resolver asks the root name servers. The roots do not know `example.com`, but they know which servers handle `.com`. The resolver asks a `.com` server. That server points to the authoritative name servers for `example.com`. The resolver asks one of those, and it returns the IP address.

Each answer carries a time-to-live value. The resolver caches the result for that many seconds. The next request for the same name skips the full chain.

DNS can return more than an A record for IPv4. It returns AAAA records for IPv6, MX records for mail servers, CNAME records for aliases, and other types. The resolver returns the records the client asked for.

If a name does not exist, the authoritative server says so. If the resolver cannot reach the servers, the lookup times out.

A deadlock is a standoff between two or more threads where each one holds a lock the next one needs, and none can proceed.

Picture two threads, A and B, and two locks, X and Y. Thread A locks X, then tries to lock Y. Thread B locks Y, then tries to lock X. A waits for Y, which B holds. B waits for X, which A holds. Both wait forever.

One way to avoid it is lock ordering. Every thread acquires the same locks in the same order. If both A and B always lock X before Y, then B cannot hold Y while waiting for X, and the cycle cannot form. The order itself does not matter; only that everyone follows it.

It also hurts when the query does not match the index well. A query that returns many rows may still read most of the table; the index adds a lookup step without skipping much work. The database may choose a full table scan instead.

Indexes can also slow transactions by increasing lock contention and write amplification, especially in databases that lock index pages during modifications.

The right index is one whose query benefit exceeds its write and storage cost for that workload.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. The receiver uses those numbers to reassemble the stream in the right order.

Each TCP segment carries a sequence number. That number marks the first byte of data in the segment. The receiver acknowledges the next sequence number it expects. If segments arrive out of order, the receiver holds the early ones in a buffer until the missing byte shows up.

The sender retransmits anything it does not get an acknowledgment for within its retransmission timeout. Duplicate acknowledgments for the same sequence number tell the sender a particular segment was lost, so it resends that segment fast.

The sliding window keeps the pipe full while waiting. The receiver advertises how much buffer space it has left. The sender sends only that much unacknowledged data, then waits for acknowledgments before sliding the window forward.

This gives TCP a single in-order byte stream on top of an unreliable network that may drop, delay, or reorder packets.
