Deadlocks need four conditions: mutual exclusion, holding while waiting, no preemption, and a circular chain. Remove any one of them and the deadlock cannot form.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket chosen by the key's hash code. When two keys land in the same bucket, that is a collision.

Most implementations resolve collisions in one of two ways.

**Separate chaining** keeps a linked list inside each bucket. The bucket holds the first entry; each entry points to the next entry that hashed to the same bucket. Lookup walks the list until it finds the matching key or reaches the end. Java's `HashMap` uses this, switching list nodes to tree nodes when a bucket grows long.

**Open addressing** stores all entries directly in the table. When a slot is occupied, the probe sequence tries the next slot according to a fixed rule: linear probing checks the next slot, quadratic probing jumps by increasing squares, and double hashing uses a second hash function to set the step size. Lookup follows the same sequence.

Load factor governs performance. As the ratio of entries to slots rises, collisions cluster. Resizing copies entries into a larger table and rehashes them, which spreads them out again. The cost of one resize is high, but amortized over many insertions it stays constant.

The choice between chaining and open addressing trades memory against behavior. Chaining pays pointer overhead per entry but tolerates high load factors and deletion cleanly. Open addressing avoids pointers but suffers from clustering and needs tombstones or rehashing on deletion.

A database index is a separate, smaller structure that points to rows in a table so the database can find them without reading every row.

Most indexes are B-trees. They store the indexed column values in sorted order, with leaf nodes holding pointers to the actual row locations. A lookup on an indexed column walks the tree in O(log n) time. A full table scan reads every row in O(n) time. On a million-row table, that is roughly twenty comparisons versus a million.

Indexes help when the query filters, joins, or sorts on the indexed column. They also help enforce uniqueness and foreign-key constraints, because the database can check existence quickly.

Indexes hurt in four common ways.

First, they slow writes. Every insert, update, or delete that touches an indexed column must update the index too. A single-row insert into a table with three indexes may do four write operations instead of one.

Second, they consume space. The index holds a copy of the indexed columns plus row pointers. A wide index on a wide table can grow as large as the table itself.

Third, the optimizer sometimes chooses the index when it should not. If a query returns many rows, random I/O through the index can be slower than a sequential scan. The database may read the index, then fetch rows scattered across the table, then discard most of them. This is especially costly when the table does not fit in memory.

Fourth, indexes add maintenance. They must be rebuilt after bulk loads, and they can fragment over time. Unused indexes continue costing writes and space without helping reads.

The right index is one whose benefit to read queries outweighs its cost in writes, space, and optimizer mistakes.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. The sender assigns each byte a sequence number. The receiver acknowledges the highest contiguous sequence number it has received. If a segment arrives out of order, the receiver holds it in a buffer and repeats the last contiguous acknowledgment. The sender retransmits any segment whose acknowledgment is missing past a timeout or after three duplicate acknowledgments. The receiver then fills the gap and delivers the now-contiguous bytes to the application in order.

A mutex protects a program against race conditions on shared data.

A race condition happens when two threads read and write the same memory at the same time, and the final result depends on the order their instructions interleave. A mutex prevents that interleaving inside the protected region.

When a thread wants to enter the region, it calls `lock`. If no other thread holds the mutex, the caller proceeds. If another thread holds it, the caller waits. When the holder leaves, it calls `unlock`, and exactly one waiting thread wakes up and enters.

Only one thread can hold the mutex at a time. That turns the critical section into a sequence of single-threaded steps. A counter update, a linked-list insert, or a buffer write completes before another thread starts the same operation.

A mutex does not protect against every concurrency bug. It does not prevent deadlocks if threads acquire multiple mutexes in different orders. It does not prevent a thread from accessing the data without locking. It only enforces mutual exclusion for threads that use it correctly.

A garbage collector finds unused memory by tracing what the program can still reach.

It starts from roots: local variables on thread stacks, global variables, and CPU registers that hold references. These are the objects the program can touch right now.

From each root, it follows every pointer field to other objects, and from those objects to more objects. Every object it reaches is alive. Anything it never reaches is garbage.

Mark-and-sweep collectors do this in two passes. The mark pass walks the live graph and sets a bit on each reachable object. The sweep pass scans the heap and returns unmarked objects to free memory.

Generational collectors exploit one fact: most objects die young. They divide the heap into generations. New objects go in a nursery. Frequent minor collections scan only the nursery and move survivors to an older generation. Major collections scan the whole heap less often.

Some collectors use reference counting instead. Each object stores a count of incoming references. When the count drops to zero, the object is unused. Reference counting reclaims memory immediately, but it cannot collect cycles: two objects that point only to each other keep each other's count above zero.

Tracing collectors stop the program to do their work, or they run concurrently and track pointer changes with write barriers. The tradeoff is pause length against throughput and implementation complexity.

A race condition is a bug where two threads read and write the same data at overlapping times, and the final result depends on the exact order their instructions run.

Here is a concrete example. Two threads each increment a shared counter by one. The counter starts at 0. Each thread does three steps: read the value, add one, write the value back. Thread A reads 0. Before A writes 1, thread B reads 0. A writes 1. B writes 1. The counter ends at 1, not 2. Both increments happened, but one update overwrote the other.

The bug is not that the threads run at the same time; it is that the read-modify-write sequence is not atomic. The outcome changes with timing. On some runs the counter reaches 2; on others it stays at 1. That nondeterminism makes the bug hard to reproduce and hard to test.

A mutex fixes this by making the increment a single indivisible block. Only one thread can hold the lock while it reads, adds, and writes. The second thread waits until the first finishes, so the counter reliably becomes 2.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping recently used memory close to the processor.

Main memory sits far from the cores, on separate chips connected by a bus. A fetch from DRAM can take a hundred nanoseconds or more. The cache is smaller memory made of faster transistors, placed on the same die as the CPU. A hit in the L1 cache returns data in a handful of clock cycles.

Programs tend to access memory with two kinds of locality. Temporal locality means a byte used once is likely to be used again soon. Spatial locality means a byte used is likely to be near another byte that will be used next. The cache exploits both: it keeps recently accessed data, and it fetches whole cache lines, typically 64 bytes at a time, hoping the neighboring bytes will be needed.

When the CPU reads an address, it checks the cache first. If the data is there, it avoids the slow trip to RAM. If it is missing, the cache loads the whole line from memory and stores it. Writes work similarly: the cache may write through to memory immediately or write back later when the line is evicted.

Caches are organized in levels. L1 is smallest and fastest, often split into instruction and data caches. L2 is larger and slower. L3 is larger still and shared across cores. A request that misses L1 may hit L2 or L3 before falling all the way to DRAM.

The speedup is not guaranteed. A program that jumps randomly through a large working set misses the cache repeatedly and performs nearly as if no cache existed. A program that walks arrays sequentially or reuses small structures keeps its data in cache and runs many times faster.

An HTTP request is idempotent when making it once and making it many times produce the same result on the server.

A `GET` request is idempotent because it only reads. Calling it ten times returns the same resource and changes nothing.

A `PUT` request that replaces a user's name with "Alice" is idempotent. The first call sets the name to "Alice". The second call sets the name to "Alice" again. The server ends in the same state.

A `POST` request that creates a new order is usually not idempotent. If the client sends it twice because the first response timed out, the server may create two orders. The state changes with each call.

Idempotency matters when networks fail. A client cannot tell whether a lost response means the request failed or the reply failed. It can safely retry an idempotent request. It must not blindly retry a non-idempotent one.

Some APIs make `POST` idempotent by having the client send a unique idempotency key. The server stores the key and ignores duplicate requests that carry the same key. Stripe's API works this way.

HTTP defines `GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `OPTIONS`, and `TRACE` as idempotent by specification. `POST` and `PATCH` are not, though a particular implementation can make them so.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a chain of servers, each one more specific than the last.

A browser or program starts with a stub resolver on the local machine. The stub resolver checks its cache. If the address is not there, it sends a query to a recursive resolver, usually run by the operating system, the router, or a service like Google DNS at 8.8.8.8.

The recursive resolver asks the root servers. Thirteen logical root servers, named A through M, know where the top-level domains live. The resolver asks a root server for `example.com`. The root server does not know the address, but it returns a referral to the servers for `.com`.

The resolver then asks a `.com` server. That server does not know `example.com` either, but it returns a referral to the name servers that handle `example.com`.

The resolver asks one of those name servers. This server holds the zone file for `example.com`. It returns the A record, which contains the IPv4 address, or the AAAA record for IPv6.

The recursive resolver caches the answer and returns it to the stub resolver, which returns it to the program. Each record has a time-to-live value that tells resolvers how long they may keep it.

If the name does not exist, the authoritative server returns an NXDOMAIN response. If the server is unreachable, the resolver retries or returns a failure.

The whole chain keeps the distributed database manageable. No single server stores every name. Each level delegates to the next, and caching keeps repeated queries from hammering the root.

A deadlock is a standoff between threads. Each thread holds a resource the other needs, and neither releases what it has until it gets what it wants.

Picture two bank accounts and two threads. Thread A locks account 1 and waits for account 2. Thread B locks account 2 and waits for account 1. Both wait forever.

One way to avoid this is to lock resources in a fixed global order. Every thread must acquire account 1 before account 2. Then A and B cannot hold each other's next target. One thread reaches the shared first lock and proceeds; the other waits, but it waits on a lock that will be released.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket chosen by the key's hash code. When two keys land in the same bucket, the map has a collision.

Most hash maps resolve collisions by chaining. Each bucket holds a linked list or tree of entries that share that bucket. A lookup hashes the key, walks the list at that bucket, and compares keys with `equals` until it finds a match.

Open addressing is the other common approach. It stores every entry inside the table array itself. When a bucket is full, the probe continues to the next slot—linear, quadratic, or by a second hash—until it finds the key or an empty slot.

Chaining keeps the table simple at low load but degrades as lists grow. Open addressing uses less memory per entry but suffers from clustering and needs a low load factor.

Java's `HashMap` chains entries and promotes long chains to red-black trees. Python's `dict` uses open addressing with a perturbation sequence. The choice shapes memory use, worst-case lookup time, and how the table resizes.

A database index is a separate structure that points into a table's rows so the engine can find them without reading every row.

Most indexes are B-trees. The database walks the tree by the indexed column's value and reaches a leaf that stores row identifiers or the row itself. A lookup on an indexed column costs O(log n) page reads instead of a full table scan.

An index helps when a query filters, joins, or orders by the indexed column and the selectivity is high. It helps most on large tables with selective `WHERE` clauses.

An index hurts in four common ways:

- **Writes slow down.** Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` must update the index as well as the table. On a table with many indexes, a simple insert can become several random writes.
- **It takes space.** The index file can grow as large as the table, sometimes larger.
- **The optimizer may choose it wrongly.** If the query returns most of the table, an index lookup plus row fetches can cost more than a sequential scan. The planner's cost estimate, not the index itself, decides.
- **It adds lock contention and maintenance.** Rebuilding, splitting pages, and keeping statistics current consume I/O and can block or slow concurrent work.

Indexes also hurt when they are unused but still maintained, or when they duplicate another index with a slightly different column order.

The right index is one the workload actually uses and cannot satisfy with a cheaper plan.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. The receiver uses those numbers to reassemble the stream in the right order and to detect gaps.

Each TCP segment carries a sequence number for its first byte. The receiver acknowledges the next expected byte with an ACK. If a segment arrives out of order, the receiver holds it in a buffer until the missing bytes show up. It does not deliver data to the application until the gap closes.

The sender retransmits anything it has not acknowledged within its retransmission timeout, or when it gets three duplicate ACKs. Selective acknowledgment lets the receiver report exactly which blocks it has received, so the sender retransmits only the missing pieces.

The result is a single in-order byte stream to the application, even when the network delivers packets out of order, drops them, or duplicates them.

A mutex protects a program against race conditions on shared data.

A race condition happens when two threads read and write the same memory without ordering, and the final value depends on which thread runs first. A mutex is a lock. One thread acquires it before touching the shared data. The operating system or runtime lets only one thread hold the lock at a time. Other threads that try to acquire it wait until the holder releases it.

The mutex does not remove the shared data. It serializes access to it. Every thread that reads or writes the data must follow the same rule: acquire, use, release. If one thread skips the lock, the protection breaks for all of them.

A mutex also prevents torn updates. On most hardware, writing a 64-bit pointer or integer is not atomic. A lock makes the whole critical section atomic with respect to other threads that use the same lock.

It does not prevent deadlocks by itself. If thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2 while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1, both wait forever. Ordering lock acquisition fixes that.

A mutex is the wrong tool for read-only data, data owned by one thread, or operations that can run lock-free with atomic instructions. Use it where multiple threads must mutate the same state and the cost of occasional waiting is acceptable.

A hash map resolves collisions by storing more than one entry in the same bucket.

Most implementations use chaining. Each bucket holds a list or tree of entries whose keys share that bucket. A lookup hashes the key, walks the list, and compares keys with `equals` until it finds a match.

Open addressing stores every entry inside the table array. When a bucket is full, the probe continues to the next slot—linear, quadratic, or by a second hash—until it finds the key or an empty slot.

Chaining keeps the table simple at low load but slows as lists grow. Open addressing uses less memory per entry but clusters badly and needs a low load factor.

Java's `HashMap` chains entries and turns long chains into red-black trees. Python's `dict` uses open addressing with a perturbation sequence. The choice shapes memory use, worst-case lookup time, and how the table resizes.

A race condition is a bug where two threads touch the same data at the same time and the outcome depends on which thread wins.

Imagine two cashiers updating the same bank balance. The balance is $100. Thread A reads $100 and adds $50. Thread B reads $100 and subtracts $20. A writes $150. B writes $80. The final balance is $80, not $130. One update vanished.

The race happens because the read-modify-write is not atomic. Each thread saw the old value, changed it, and wrote back without seeing the other's work.

A mutex fixes it by letting only one thread hold the balance at a time. Atomic instructions can also fix it for simple operations. The fix must cover every path that touches the shared data; one unlocked path breaks the protection for all paths.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping recently used memory close to the processor.

Most programs reuse the same small set of memory locations repeatedly. A cache stores copies of those locations in fast SRAM on the CPU die. When the processor needs data, it checks the cache first. A hit returns the data in a few cycles. A miss fetches it from main memory, which can take hundreds of cycles.

Caches exploit two patterns. Temporal locality means a location used once is likely to be used again soon. Spatial locality means a location near one just used is likely to be used next. The cache therefore fetches whole cache lines, typically 64 bytes, not single bytes.

A modern CPU has multiple levels. L1 is smallest and fastest, often split into instruction and data caches. L2 is larger and slower. L3 is shared across cores and slower still. Data flows from disk to RAM to L3 to L2 to L1 to registers.

A cache speeds up only when the working set fits. If the program jumps through memory randomly, every access misses and the cache adds overhead without benefit. If the program scans an array sequentially, most accesses hit and run at cache speed, not memory speed.

Idempotency means an API call produces the same result whether it runs once or many times.

A client sends `PUT /users/42` with the same payload twice. The first request creates or updates the record. The second request leaves the record in the same state and returns the same response. The server does not add a second user or change the balance.

Safe methods like `GET` and `HEAD` are idempotent by definition. They read state and change nothing.

`POST` is usually not idempotent. Sending `POST /orders` twice creates two orders. To make it idempotent, the client includes a unique idempotency key. The server stores the key with the result and returns the stored result for repeats.

Idempotency helps retries. Networks drop packets and clients resend. An idempotent endpoint handles the retry without duplicate work. It also simplifies recovery: the client can call again without checking first.

The server must still enforce it. A repeated request with the same key must return the same response and must not run side effects twice. The key needs a timeout, or the server will store results forever.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a chain of resolvers, each one closer to the source of truth.

A browser or application first asks a stub resolver, usually inside the operating system. The stub resolver checks its cache. If the answer is not there, it sends a query to a recursive resolver, often run by the ISP or a public service like Cloudflare or Google.

The recursive resolver also checks its cache. If it has no answer, it starts at the root. It asks one of the thirteen logical root name servers for the address of the top-level domain server, such as the server for `.com`. It then asks that TLD server for the address of the authoritative name server for the domain, such as `example.com`. Finally, it asks that authoritative server for the record that maps the full name, such as `www.example.com`, to an IP address.

Each reply carries a time-to-live. The resolver stores the answer for that many seconds before asking again.

If the record is a `CNAME`, the resolver follows the alias and repeats the lookup. If the record is an `A` record, it returns an IPv4 address. If it is an `AAAA` record, it returns an IPv6 address.

The application then opens a connection to that address.

A deadlock is a standoff between two or more threads, each holding a resource the others need and waiting for a resource the others hold.

Thread A locks account X and waits for account Y. Thread B locks account Y and waits for account X. Neither releases; neither proceeds.

One way to avoid it is to order every lock acquisition globally. Every thread must acquire locks in the same sequence—say, always the lower-numbered account first. With a fixed order, no cycle can form, and a deadlock cannot occur.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket numbered by the key's hash code. When two keys land in the same bucket, the map has a collision.

Most hash maps chain colliding entries. Each bucket holds a linked list, array, or tree of entries that share that bucket. A lookup first computes the bucket index from the key's hash, then scans the entries in that bucket for an exact key match.

Java's `HashMap` uses linked lists by default and switches a bucket to a balanced tree when the list grows past eight entries. Python's `dict` uses open addressing instead: it probes a sequence of slots until it finds the key or an empty slot. Both approaches keep average lookup time near O(1) when the hash function spreads keys evenly.

A poor hash function clusters many keys into a few buckets and degrades lookup to O(n). Resizing the table—doubling the bucket count and reinserting entries—reduces load and keeps chains short.

A database index is a separate, ordered copy of a column or columns that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table.

The database builds the index as a B-tree, a sorted tree structure. A lookup walks the tree in O(log n) time and reaches the exact row pointer. Without the index, the database reads every row and compares values one by one.

Indexes help when queries filter, sort, or join on the indexed column. A query like `WHERE last_name = 'Smith'` uses the index to fetch only matching rows. A primary key lookup is the fastest case: the database goes straight to one row.

Indexes hurt in three ways.

First, they slow writes. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` must update both the table and every index that covers the changed columns. A table with six indexes can turn a simple insert into six tree updates plus the row write.

Second, they consume space. The index stores the indexed values plus row pointers, and large text columns or composite indexes make it bulky. A full-text index on a big table can exceed the table's own size.

Third, the database may ignore the index and scan the table anyway. If a query returns a large fraction of rows, scanning is cheaper than bouncing between index and table. A query like `WHERE status <> 'archived'` on a mostly-unarchived table usually triggers a full scan. The query planner decides this based on statistics, and bad statistics or stale histograms make it choose wrong.

Indexes also hurt when they exist but are unusable. A query with a function on the column, like `WHERE UPPER(email) = 'X'`, cannot use a plain index on `email`. A leading wildcard, `WHERE name LIKE '%son'`, defeats a B-tree index. A composite index on `(a, b, c)` helps only when the query filters from the left: `a`, `a and b`, or `a and b and c`. Filtering only on `c` skips the index.

The right index is one the workload actually uses. An unused index is pure cost: it slows writes and takes disk space without speeding reads.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. The receiver uses those numbers to reassemble the stream in the right order and to detect gaps.

Each TCP segment carries a sequence number. That number marks the first byte of data in the segment. The receiver acknowledges the next sequence number it expects. If segment 100–199 arrives before segment 50–99, the receiver holds 100–199 in a buffer and waits for 50–99. Once the missing segment arrives, TCP releases the in-order bytes to the application.

The sender retransmits anything it does not get an acknowledgment for within its retransmission timeout. Duplicate acknowledgments for the same sequence number, or a timeout, trigger the resend. The receiver discards duplicates by checking sequence numbers.

This sequence-and-acknowledgment system gives TCP its ordered, reliable byte stream.

A mutex protects a program against race conditions on shared data.

When two threads read and write the same variable without coordination, the final value depends on the exact order of instructions. That order changes from run to run. A mutex prevents this by letting only one thread enter a critical section at a time.

The thread that wants the data calls `lock`. If no other thread holds the mutex, it proceeds. If another thread holds it, the caller waits. The thread leaves the section and calls `unlock`, which wakes a waiting thread.

Without a mutex, a read-modify-write operation can interleave. Two threads can both read a counter as 5, both add 1, and both write 6. The counter ends at 6 instead of 7. A mutex makes the increment atomic relative to other threads.

A mutex does not protect against deadlocks. Two threads can each lock one resource and wait for the other. It also does not protect against bugs inside the critical section, where one thread reads invalid state written by itself.

The cost is contention: threads spend time waiting, and the lock itself takes memory and CPU cycles. A coarse lock is easy to reason about but serializes more work. A fine-grained lock reduces waiting but raises the risk of deadlock and makes the code harder to maintain.

Garbage collection starts from the objects the program can still reach.

The collector marks every object reachable from live roots: local variables on thread stacks, global variables, and CPU registers that hold references. It follows each reference recursively. Any object it reaches is marked live.

After marking, the collector sweeps the heap. It reclaims every object the mark phase did not reach. These objects have no path from any root, so the program cannot use them again.

Some collectors add a compacting step. They move live objects together and update the references that point to them. This removes gaps between objects and keeps free memory in one contiguous block.

Generational collectors exploit one observed fact: most objects die young. They divide the heap into generations and scan the young generation more often. Objects that survive several collections move to an older generation, which the collector scans less frequently.

The tradeoff is pause time. Marking and sweeping must stop the program, or coordinate with it, so references do not change underneath the collector. Concurrent and incremental collectors reduce pauses by doing part of the work while the program runs, but they add bookkeeping and sometimes leave some garbage to a later cycle.

A race condition is a bug where the outcome depends on the exact order in which two threads execute their instructions.

Consider two threads that increment the same counter. The counter starts at 0. Each thread reads the value, adds 1, and writes it back. Thread A reads 0. Before A writes 1, Thread B reads 0. Both threads write 1. The counter ends at 1, not 2.

The problem is the read-add-write sequence is not atomic. The operating system can switch between A and B at any point. Some interleavings produce the correct result; others do not. The program behaves differently from run to run.

A mutex prevents this by allowing only one thread to hold the lock while it reads and writes the counter. The second thread waits until the first releases the lock. The increment then completes before the next begins, and the counter reaches 2.

A CPU cache speeds a program by keeping recently used memory close to the core, where fetch latency is lower.

When a core reads a variable, the hardware first checks the L1 cache, a small SRAM bank on the same die. A hit there returns data in a few cycles. A miss goes to L2, then L3, then main memory, each step adding tens to hundreds of cycles. Main memory is DRAM, slower because it lives off-chip and needs refresh cycles.

Caches exploit locality. Temporal locality means a byte used once is likely used again soon; the cache keeps it. Spatial locality means a byte used is near others that will be used next; the cache fetches a whole 64-byte line, not just the requested word.

A multi-core chip shares the last-level cache and keeps separate L1 caches. When one core writes a line, the cache-coherence protocol invalidates or updates copies in other cores so no stale value is read. False sharing occurs when two cores write different variables that happen to sit on the same cache line, forcing the line to bounce between cores and negating the speedup.

A cache also speeds code. Loops that fit in the instruction cache run without waiting for memory. Sequential access through an array lets the hardware prefetch the next lines. Random pointer chasing, by contrast, misses often and waits for memory at every step.

The gain is not uniform. A program with a small working set may run at cache speed; one that thrashes across gigabytes is limited by DRAM bandwidth and latency.

Idempotency means an HTTP request produces the same server state no matter how many times a client sends it.

A client sends a `PUT` request to `/users/123` with `{ "email": "a@b.com" }`. The server updates the user and returns `200 OK`. If the client sends the same `PUT` again, the email stays `a@b.com` and the server returns `200 OK`. The state does not change further.

A `POST` to `/charges` that creates a new charge each time is not idempotent. Two retries create two charges. An idempotent `POST` includes an idempotency key, such as `Idempotency-Key: abc-123`. The server stores the result for that key. A retry with the same key returns the stored result instead of creating another charge.

Safe methods like `GET`, `HEAD`, and `OPTIONS` are idempotent by definition: they do not change state at all. `DELETE` is idempotent because deleting the same resource twice leaves it deleted; the second call usually returns `404` or `204`, but the resource is gone either way.

Idempotency helps networks. Requests can time out or retry. Without it, a retry might book two flights or bill a card twice. With it, the server recognizes the duplicate and returns the same answer.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a chain of name servers, each one more specific than the last.

A program starts with a resolver, usually inside the operating system or a library. The resolver first checks its own cache. If the answer is there, it returns immediately. If not, it sends a query to a recursive resolver, often run by the ISP or a public service like Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 or Google's 8.8.8.8.

That recursive resolver asks the root name servers. There are thirteen logical root servers, and they know only where the top-level domain servers live. The root server answers with the addresses for the servers that handle `.com`, `.org`, `.net`, or whatever suffix the name carries.

The recursive resolver then asks the top-level domain server for the name. The `.com` server does not know the final address either, but it knows which name server is authoritative for the specific domain. It returns the address of that authoritative server.

The recursive resolver asks the authoritative server. This server holds the actual record, such as an A record that maps the name to an IPv4 address or an AAAA record for IPv6. It returns the address.

The recursive resolver hands the answer back to the program and caches it. The cache honors a time-to-live value set by the record's owner, after which the resolver must ask again.

Each step uses UDP for the query when the response is small; TCP handles larger replies or zone transfers. The whole chain normally completes in milliseconds, and the program never sees the intermediate steps.

A deadlock is a standoff between two or more threads, each holding a resource the other needs.

Picture two threads and two locks. Thread A locks the account file. Thread B locks the log file. Thread A then tries to lock the log file and waits. Thread B tries to lock the account file and waits. Neither releases what it holds. Neither gets what it wants. They stay stuck.

One way to avoid this is to lock resources in a fixed order. Every thread that needs both the account file and the log file must lock the account file first, then the log file. Thread B, wanting the log file first, would instead take the account file first. The circular wait disappears, and the deadlock cannot form.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket numbered by the key's hash code. When two keys land in the same bucket, the map has a collision.

Most hash maps resolve collisions by chaining: each bucket holds a linked list of entries that share that bucket number. A lookup hashes the key, walks the list at that bucket, and compares keys until it finds a match.

Open addressing is the other common method. It stores entries directly in the table array. When a bucket is full, the probe sequence tries the next slot—linear probing checks the following index, quadratic probing jumps by increasing squares, and double hashing uses a second hash function to set the step size.

Chaining keeps the table simple but pays pointer overhead per entry. Open addressing avoids pointers but can cluster entries and needs careful load-factor limits. A well-built hash map rehashes into a larger table when the ratio of entries to buckets grows too high, keeping collisions rare.

A database index is a separate data structure that points to rows in a table, built on one or more columns so the database can find rows without scanning every page.

The most common index is a B-tree. It stores column values in sorted order, with leaf nodes containing pointers to the actual row locations. A lookup on an indexed column walks the tree in O(log n) page reads instead of reading the entire table.

Indexes hurt when they are wrong for the query. A query that filters on an unindexed column or uses a function on the indexed column cannot use the index and falls back to a full scan. An index on a column with low cardinality—like a boolean flag—returns many rows and may be slower than a scan because of the extra pointer hops.

They also hurt on write-heavy tables. Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` must update every relevant index, and each update is a random I/O operation. A table with six indexes does six times the write work.

Indexes cost disk space and memory. A wide index on a large text column can exceed the size of the table itself. If the index does not fit in memory, lookups spill to disk and lose their speed advantage.

Finally, a bad query plan may choose the index when it should not. The optimizer estimates row counts from statistics; stale statistics can make it pick a nested-loop over an index when a sequential scan would finish faster.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. Each segment carries a sequence number that marks where its data belongs in the stream.

The receiver acknowledges the highest contiguous sequence number it has received. If segment three arrives before segment two, the receiver holds segment three in a buffer and repeats its acknowledgment for the last in-order byte. The sender keeps segment two and retransmits it when the acknowledgment does not advance.

This sequence-and-acknowledge loop, plus the receiver's reassembly buffer, keeps the byte stream in order even when the network delivers packets out of sequence or drops some entirely.

A mutex protects a program against race conditions on shared data.

A race condition happens when two threads read and write the same memory at the same time. Thread A might read a value, thread B might overwrite it, and thread A might then write back a stale result. The final state depends on which thread wins, and that outcome can change from run to run.

A mutex is a lock. One thread acquires it before entering a critical section. While that thread holds the lock, every other thread that tries to acquire the same mutex blocks until the lock is released. This serializes access: the protected code runs by one thread at a time.

The mutex does not protect the data by itself. The programmer must acquire the right mutex before every read or write of the shared state. If one path forgets the lock, the race condition returns.

A mutex also prevents torn writes. On most hardware, writing a 64-bit pointer is not atomic. Without a lock, one thread might see half of an old pointer and half of a new one. A mutex makes such reads and writes atomic with respect to other threads that use the same lock.

Mutexes can deadlock. Thread 1 holds lock A and waits for lock B; thread 2 holds lock B and waits for lock A. Both wait forever. The fix is usually a fixed lock order: always acquire A before B.

A mutex trades concurrency for correctness. It does not make code faster; it makes shared-state code safe enough to run in parallel.

Garbage collection finds unused memory by tracing reachable objects from a set of roots.

The roots are the starting points: local variables on thread stacks, global variables, and CPU registers that hold references. The collector marks every object that the roots can reach, directly or through other objects.

It begins with the roots and follows each reference. If object A points to object B, the collector marks B and then follows B's references. This continues until no new objects are reachable.

Any object the collector did not mark is unreachable from the running program. The program cannot use that object again, so the collector reclaims its memory.

Some collectors add a reference count to each object. The count rises when a new reference is created and falls when a reference is removed. When the count hits zero, the object has no live references and the collector frees it immediately. Reference counting cannot reclaim cycles: if object X points to Y and Y points back to X, both counts stay above zero even when nothing else references them.

Tracing collectors handle cycles because they care about reachability, not the number of references. Generational collectors take advantage of the observation that most objects die young. They divide the heap into generations and scan the young generation more often, moving survivors to older generations.

The tradeoff is pauses. A stop-the-world collector pauses all program threads while it traces the heap. Concurrent collectors run some of their work alongside the program, reducing pauses but adding complexity and sometimes reclaiming memory later.

A race condition is a bug where the result of a program depends on the exact timing of two or more threads.

Picture two clerks updating the same ledger. The ledger shows a balance of 100. Clerk A reads 100, adds 10, and intends to write 110. Clerk B reads 100 at the same time, subtracts 20, and intends to write 80. A writes 110. B writes 80. The final balance is 80, and A's deposit is gone. If B had written first, the result would be 110. The program's output changes with the order of execution.

In code, the same thing happens when two threads update a shared counter without coordination. Thread 1 loads the value into a register, increments it, and stores it back. Thread 2 does the same. Each read-modify-write is three separate steps. The operating system can switch threads between any two steps, so the increments can overlap and one update can overwrite the other.

The bug is not that the threads run at the same time; it is that the program has no mechanism to make the read-modify-write sequence atomic. A mutex, an atomic increment, or a compare-and-swap loop fixes it by forcing the steps to complete without interruption.

Race conditions are hard to test because they often pass. The scheduler may run the threads in the lucky order a thousand times and fail only under load, on a different machine, or after a code change shifts the timing.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping recently used memory close to the processor.

Main memory sits far from the CPU, and a trip there costs dozens or hundreds of clock cycles. The cache is a smaller, faster memory bank between the CPU and main RAM. When the CPU reads an address, the hardware copies a whole block of neighboring bytes into the cache. Later reads to the same block or nearby bytes hit the cache and finish in a few cycles instead of waiting for RAM.

Programs spend much of their time reusing a small working set of data and instructions. The cache exploits this locality. Temporal locality means a byte accessed once is likely accessed again soon. Spatial locality means a byte accessed is likely near other bytes the program will touch next.

Caches are organized in levels. L1 sits closest to each core and is the fastest but smallest, often 32 to 64 kilobytes. L2 and L3 are larger and slower, with L3 sometimes shared across all cores. A hit in L1 might take four cycles; a hit in L3 might take forty; a miss to main memory might take two hundred.

The cache also helps writes. A write-back cache stores the new value and marks the line dirty, flushing it to main memory only when the cache must make room. This batches memory traffic and avoids writing every store to RAM immediately.

Cache misses still happen, and they dominate runtime when they do. A program that jumps through memory randomly defeats spatial locality and keeps the CPU waiting. A program that reuses a compact set of data keeps the cache busy and the CPU fed.

Idempotency means an HTTP request can be sent more than once without changing the result beyond the first time.

A client might retry a `PUT` because the first response timed out. If the server already applied the update, the second `PUT` leaves the resource in the same state. The client does not need to know whether the first attempt reached the server.

`GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` are normally idempotent. Calling `DELETE /orders/42` twice removes the order once; the second call returns `404` and the order is still gone.

`POST` is usually not idempotent. Two `POST /charges` requests create two charges. A retry without a guard duplicates the side effect.

Safe methods are a related but narrower idea. `GET` is both safe and idempotent: it changes nothing, and repeating it changes nothing again. `PUT` is idempotent but not safe, because it does change state.

APIs sometimes add idempotency keys for `POST`. The client sends a unique key with the request; the server stores the key and ignores repeats. Stripe uses this to prevent double-charging when a network error makes a client retry.

Idempotency does not mean the response is identical each time. The first `DELETE` returns `200`; the second returns `404`. The server state stays the same, and that is the point.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a chain of name servers.

When a browser needs `example.com`, the resolver on the machine first checks its own cache. If the name is not there, it sends the query to a recursive resolver, usually run by the ISP or a public service like Cloudflare's `1.1.1.1` or Google's `8.8.8.8`.

The recursive resolver asks a root server. The root does not know `example.com`, but it points the resolver to the servers for the `.com` zone. The resolver asks a `.com` server, which points it to the authoritative name servers for `example.com`. The resolver asks one of those, and that server returns the IP address.

Each reply carries a time-to-live value. The resolver caches the result for that many seconds, so later lookups for the same name do not repeat the full chain.

If the authoritative server returns multiple addresses, the resolver may pick one or hand them all back to the client. The client then opens a connection to that address.

A deadlock is a standoff between two or more threads, each holding a resource the other needs and waiting for the other to release it first.

Picture two trucks on a narrow bridge. Truck A enters from the north and stops because Truck B is coming from the south. Truck B stops because Truck A is in the way. Neither can back up, so neither moves.

In a program, the resources are usually locks. Thread 1 acquires lock A and then tries to acquire lock B. Thread 2 acquires lock B and then tries to acquire lock A. Thread 1 waits for B, which Thread 2 holds. Thread 2 waits for A, which Thread 1 holds. Both wait forever.

One way to avoid this is to make every thread acquire locks in the same order. If both threads always take A before B, Thread 2 cannot hold B while waiting for A, because it would have needed A first. The fixed order removes the circular wait, and the deadlock cannot form.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket numbered by the key's hash code. When two keys land in the same bucket, that is a collision.

Most hash maps resolve collisions by chaining. Each bucket holds a linked list or tree of entries. A lookup hashes the key, walks that bucket's chain, and compares keys until it finds a match.

Open addressing is the other common method. It stores every entry directly in the table array. When a bucket is full, the map probes forward—linearly, quadratically, or by a second hash—until it finds an empty slot. Lookup follows the same probe sequence.

Load factor governs performance. Chaining slows as buckets grow long; open addressing slows as clusters form. A hash map typically resizes and rehashes all entries into a larger array once the load factor crosses a threshold, often around 0.75.

Java's `HashMap` uses chaining and converts long chains into balanced trees. Python's `dict` uses open addressing with a probe sequence derived from the hash. The choice trades memory against worst-case lookup time.

A database index is a separate, smaller structure that points to rows in a table, built on one or more columns so the database can find matching rows without scanning the whole table.

An index helps when the query filters, sorts, or joins on the indexed columns. A B-tree index, the most common kind, keeps values in sorted order; it can locate a value in O(log n) page reads instead of reading every row. It also lets the database return sorted results without a separate sort step.

An index hurts when maintaining it costs more than it saves. Every insert, update, or delete on the table must also update every index on that table. A table with many indexes writes slowly. Indexes also consume disk space and memory; a wide index on a small table may be slower than a full table scan because reading the index and then fetching rows adds random I/O. The query planner may ignore an index if the selectivity is low, such as an index on a boolean column where half the rows match.

Indexes hurt especially on write-heavy workloads, on columns that change frequently, and on low-cardinality columns that do not narrow the result set. They also hurt when they exist but the query cannot use them, because the database still pays to keep them current.

A TCP sender numbers every byte it sends. The receiver uses those sequence numbers to reassemble the stream in the right order, even if packets arrive out of sequence.

Each TCP segment carries a sequence number for its first byte and an acknowledgment number for the next byte the receiver expects. The receiver buffers out-of-order segments and waits for the missing one. It sends duplicate acknowledgments for the gap, which tells the sender to retransmit.

The sender keeps unacknowledged bytes in its retransmission queue. A timeout or three duplicate ACKs triggers a retransmission. The receiver then fills the hole and advances the in-order stream to the application.

This sequence-and-ack mechanism replaces a missing packet without the application seeing gaps or duplicates.

A mutex protects a program against race conditions on shared data.

A race condition happens when two threads read and write the same memory at the same time, and the final result depends on the order their operations interleave. A mutex prevents that by letting only one thread enter a critical section at a time.

The thread that wants the shared data calls `lock`. If the mutex is free, the thread takes it and proceeds. If another thread already holds it, the caller waits until the holder calls `unlock`. That serializes access: the operations inside the critical section never overlap.

Without a mutex, two threads can both read a counter, both add one, and both write back the old value plus one. The counter increments once instead of twice. A mutex makes the read-add-write sequence atomic with respect to other threads.

A mutex does not protect against deadlocks. If thread A holds mutex 1 and waits for mutex 2 while thread B holds mutex 2 and waits for mutex 1, both wait forever. It also does not protect against a thread accessing the data without locking. The correctness depends on every thread taking the mutex before touching the shared state.

A garbage collector finds unused memory by tracing which objects the running program can still reach.

Most collectors start from a set of roots: local variables on thread stacks, global variables, and CPU registers that hold references. They mark every object reachable from a root, then follow references inside those objects to mark more. Anything left unmarked is unreachable and can be reclaimed.

Reference counting is a different approach. Each object stores a count of incoming references; when the count drops to zero, the object is unused. It reclaims memory immediately but cannot collect cycles—two objects that point only to each other keep each other alive.

Generational collectors exploit a real pattern: most objects die young. They divide the heap into generations and scan the young generation often, since it produces most garbage. Objects that survive several collections move to an older generation, which the collector scans less frequently.

A tracing collector may pause the program to mark and sweep, or it may run concurrently with careful barriers that track references changed while the collector works. The tradeoff is between pause length, total CPU overhead, and memory fragmentation.

A race condition is a bug where the outcome depends on the timing or order of operations that run concurrently.

Picture two threads sharing a counter. The counter starts at 0. Each thread reads the value, adds 1, and writes it back. Thread A reads 0. Before A writes, thread B reads 0. A writes 1. B writes 1. The counter ends at 1, not 2. The threads did not corrupt memory; they simply overlapped in a way the program did not anticipate.

The cause is a non-atomic read-modify-write sequence. The read and the write are separate steps, and another thread can slip between them.

A race condition differs from a deadlock. A deadlock is two threads waiting on each other; a race condition is two threads racing to change the same state. Mutexes, atomic operations, and careful ordering prevent races by making the critical sequence indivisible.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping recently used memory close to the processor.

Main memory sits far enough away that a fetch can take hundreds of clock cycles. A cache is a smaller, faster memory bank between the CPU and RAM. When the CPU needs a byte, it first checks the cache. A hit returns the data in a few cycles. A miss fetches a whole cache line from RAM and stores it nearby.

Programs tend to reuse data they just touched, and they tend to access nearby addresses next. Caches exploit both habits. They keep hot values ready and pull in neighboring bytes on every miss.

Caches usually come in levels. L1 sits inside each core and is the fastest but smallest. L2 is larger and slightly slower. L3 is shared across cores and larger still. The CPU searches L1, then L2, then L3, then RAM.

A cache miss still costs the full RAM latency. So a program that jumps around memory, touching one byte per cache line and never returning, gains little. A program that walks an array sequentially reuses almost every fetched line and runs much faster.

Idempotency means an HTTP request can be sent more than once without changing the result beyond the first time.

A `GET` request is idempotent by nature. Calling it once or ten times returns the same resource and leaves the server state unchanged.

A `PUT` request that replaces a user's name with "Lee" is idempotent. The first call sets the name to "Lee". The second call sets it to "Lee" again. The state is the same.

A `POST` request that creates a new order is usually not idempotent. Sending it twice creates two orders. The server state changes with each request.

Idempotency matters when networks fail. A client may retry a request if it never sees a response. An idempotent endpoint can be retried safely. A non-idempotent endpoint needs stronger safeguards, such as a unique idempotency key, to avoid duplicates.

HTTP defines `GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and `OPTIONS` as idempotent by specification. `POST` and `PATCH` are not guaranteed to be idempotent unless the implementation makes them so.

DNS turns a human-readable name, such as `example.com`, into an IP address a machine can reach.

A device starts with a stub resolver, usually inside the operating system. If the name is not already cached, the resolver asks a recursive resolver, often run by the ISP or a public service such as Cloudflare or Google. The recursive resolver does the walking.

The resolver first asks a root name server. The root does not know `example.com`, but it points to the servers for the `.com` top-level domain. The resolver then asks a `.com` server, which points to the authoritative name servers for `example.com`. Finally, the resolver asks one of those authoritative servers, which returns the IP address.

Each answer carries a time-to-live value. Resolvers and clients cache the result for that many seconds, so later lookups skip the walk.

If the name has a CNAME record, the resolver follows the alias and looks up the canonical name. If the query asks for an IPv6 address, it requests an AAAA record instead of an A record.

DNS is distributed, not centralized. No single server holds every name; the resolver follows referrals from root to TLD to domain until it finds the authority that actually owns the record.

A deadlock is a standoff between threads or processes that are each waiting for something another one holds.

It takes four conditions. First, each resource is held exclusively: only one thread at a time can use it. Second, a thread that already holds a resource can ask for another while keeping the first. Third, no thread can be forced to release what it holds. Fourth, the waiting threads form a circle: A waits for B, B waits for C, and C waits for A. When all four hold, nobody moves.

Picture two bank clerks updating two accounts. Clerk 1 locks account A and asks for account B. Clerk 2 already locked account B and asks for account A. Each holds one lock and waits for the other. Neither can finish, so neither releases.

One way to avoid it is to lock resources in a fixed order. If every clerk always locks the lower-numbered account first, the circular wait becomes impossible. Clerk 1 takes A, then B. Clerk 2 wants B but must take A first, which Clerk 1 already holds, so Clerk 2 waits. No circle forms, and Clerk 1 finishes and releases both.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket numbered by the key's hash code. When two keys land in the same bucket, that is a collision.

Most hash maps resolve collisions by chaining. Each bucket holds a linked list or tree of entries. A lookup hashes the key, walks that bucket's chain, and compares keys until it finds a match.

Open addressing is the other common method. It stores every entry directly in the table array. When a bucket is full, the map probes forward—linearly, quadratically, or by a second hash—until it finds an empty slot. Lookup follows the same probe sequence.

Load factor governs performance. Chaining slows as buckets grow long; open addressing slows as clusters form. A hash map typically resizes and rehashes all entries into a larger array once the load factor crosses a threshold, often around 0.75.

Java's `HashMap` uses chaining and promotes long chains to balanced trees. Python's `dict` uses open addressing with a probe sequence derived from the hash. Both resize when the table gets too crowded.

A database index is a separate data structure that points to rows so the database can find them without scanning the whole table.

Most indexes are B-trees. They store the indexed column values in sorted order, with leaf nodes holding pointers to the actual row locations. A query on an indexed column walks the tree in O(log n) time instead of reading every row.

An index helps when the query filters, sorts, or joins on the indexed column. It also helps enforce uniqueness and foreign-key constraints, because the database can check the sorted structure quickly.

An index hurts when it is unused but maintained. Every insert, update, or delete must update every relevant index, so writes slow down in proportion to the index count. Indexes consume disk space and memory. They can hurt read performance too: if a query returns most of the table, the database may still scan the table rather than bounce between the index and the heap, and a bad plan can be slower than no index at all.

Indexes hurt most on write-heavy tables with many indexes, on low-cardinality columns where the index divides the data poorly, and on small tables where a sequential scan is already fast.

TCP numbers every byte it sends. The receiver uses those numbers to reassemble the stream in the right order and to detect gaps.

Each TCP segment carries a sequence number. The receiver acknowledges the highest contiguous sequence number it has received. If segment 3 arrives before segment 2, the receiver holds segment 3 in a buffer and repeats the acknowledgment for segment 1 until segment 2 shows up. Once segment 2 arrives, the receiver fills the gap, advances the contiguous window, and sends a single acknowledgment for the new high-water mark.

The sender retransmits a segment if it does not get an acknowledgment within its retransmission timeout, or if it receives three duplicate acknowledgments for the same sequence number. Selective acknowledgment lets the receiver tell the sender exactly which out-of-order blocks it has already received, so the sender retransmits only the missing pieces.

This sequence-and-acknowledge scheme also gives TCP its reliability: lost segments are re-sent, duplicates are discarded, and the application reads the bytes in the order they were written.

A mutex protects a program against race conditions on shared data.

A race condition happens when two threads read and write the same memory at the same time, and the final result depends on the order their operations interleave. That order is unpredictable, so the program can compute wrong answers or corrupt structures.

A mutex is a lock. One thread acquires it before touching the shared data. While that thread holds the mutex, every other thread that tries to acquire the same mutex blocks and waits. Only one thread at a time runs the protected code, called the critical section. The thread releases the mutex when it is done.

This mutual exclusion turns concurrent access into serialized access around the shared resource. It does not prevent bugs inside the critical section; if the thread holding the mutex reads stale state or writes inconsistently, the data still ends up wrong.

A mutex also protects against torn updates on data larger than one atomic write. Updating a linked list, resizing a vector, or incrementing a counter made of multiple fields all need a mutex if more than one thread can do them.

Deadlock is the common risk. Thread A holds mutex 1 and waits for mutex 2 while thread B holds mutex 2 and waits for mutex 1. Lock ordering, one lock at a time, or higher-level abstractions prevent that.

A garbage collector finds unused memory by tracing reachable objects from known roots.

Roots are the starting points: local variables on thread stacks, global variables, CPU registers, and handles held by the runtime. The collector treats every object these roots can reach, directly or indirectly, as alive.

Tracing collectors start at the roots and follow references recursively. They mark each object they touch. When the walk finishes, any object without a mark is unreachable, so the collector reclaims its memory. This is mark-and-sweep.

Reference counting is a different approach. Each object stores a count of incoming references. When a new reference points to it, the count rises; when a reference disappears, the count falls. When the count hits zero, the object is unused and the collector frees it immediately. Reference counting cannot reclaim cycles of objects that point to each other but are unreachable from the roots, so runtimes that use it often add a periodic tracing collector to break cycles.

Generational collectors exploit the observation that most objects die young. They divide the heap into generations, typically young and old. New objects go in the young generation, which the collector scans frequently. Objects that survive several young-generation collections move to the old generation, which the collector scans less often. This reduces the total work because long-lived objects are not re-examined on every cycle.

A copying collector splits the young generation into two halves. It traces live objects and copies them into the other half, leaving dead objects behind. After the copy, it flips the roles of the two halves. This compacts live data and makes allocation fast because free space is contiguous.

The collector must pause the program to keep the object graph stable while it traces, or it must use incremental or concurrent techniques that track changes the program makes during the collection. Without such safeguards, the program could hide a live object from the collector by moving a reference after the collector has passed it.

A race condition is a bug where the result of a program depends on the exact timing of two or more threads.

Imagine two clerks updating the same ledger. The ledger shows a balance of 100. Clerk A reads 100, adds 10, and writes 110. Clerk B reads 100, subtracts 20, and writes 80. If B reads after A writes, the final balance is 80. If B reads before A writes, A's deposit overwrites B's withdrawal, and the final balance is 110. Both clerks did their jobs correctly, but the outcome changed because their steps interleaved differently.

The root cause is a non-atomic read-modify-write. Each clerk reads, computes, and writes as three separate steps. Another thread can slip between those steps.

A race condition is not the same as a deadlock. A deadlock is two threads waiting forever for locks each other holds. A race condition is threads finishing, but finishing wrong.

The fix is usually a lock around the read-modify-write, or an atomic operation that the hardware guarantees cannot be split. The lock turns the three steps into one indivisible block, so no thread can read stale data while another is in the middle of updating it.

A CPU cache speeds up a program by keeping recently used memory close to the processor.

A modern CPU can execute billions of operations per second, but fetching data from main memory takes hundreds of cycles. The cache is a small, fast memory bank that sits between the CPU and RAM. When the CPU reads a value, it copies a whole block of surrounding memory into the cache. If the next access hits that block, the CPU reads from cache in a few cycles instead of waiting for RAM.

Programs tend to access memory in patterns. They reuse the same variables soon after touching them, called temporal locality. They also read adjacent fields and arrays in sequence, called spatial locality. The cache exploits both. A loop that walks an array benefits because each loaded cache line covers many array elements.

Caches are organized in levels. L1 is the smallest and fastest, often 32 to 64 kilobytes per core. L2 is larger and slower. L3 is shared across cores and slower still. A typical desktop CPU might have 64 KB of L1, 512 KB of L2, and 32 MB of L3. When the CPU needs data, it checks L1, then L2, then L3, then RAM. Each miss costs more time.

A cache line is the unit of transfer, usually 64 bytes. Reading one integer pulls the whole line into cache. This helps sequential access but can waste work if the program jumps around memory and touches only one byte per line.

False sharing is one way caches hurt performance. Two cores write different variables that happen to live on the same cache line. Each write forces the other core to reload the line, even though the cores never touch the same data. The program runs slower because the hardware keeps invalidating the shared line.

Cache misses dominate runtime in many programs. A well-arranged data structure keeps hot fields together and avoids pointer chasing, so more accesses hit the cache.

Idempotency means an HTTP request can be sent more than once without changing the result beyond the first application.

A client might retry a `POST /charge` because the first response timed out. If the server already created the charge, a second request could create a duplicate. An idempotent endpoint prevents that. The client includes an idempotency key, such as `Idempotency-Key: 7b3f-9a2c`, in the header. The server stores the key with the response. If the same key arrives again, the server returns the stored response instead of re-running the charge.

Safe methods are idempotent by definition. `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, and `TRACE` should not change server state, so repeating them leaves the resource unchanged. `PUT` and `DELETE` are also meant to be idempotent: sending `PUT /users/42` with the same body twice sets the user to the same state; sending `DELETE /users/42` twice leaves the user deleted.

`POST` is the usual exception. It is designed to create or process something, and a retry without a key often creates a second resource. That is why payment and booking APIs require idempotency keys on `POST`.

Idempotency does not mean the response is identical each time. The first `DELETE` returns `204 No Content`; the second may return `404 Not Found` because the resource is already gone. Both are correct because the server state ends up the same.

DNS turns a name into an address by asking a hierarchy of servers, each one closer to the answer.

A browser or program starts with a resolver, usually run by the operating system or the local network. The resolver first checks its cache. If the name is there, it returns the address immediately.

If not, the resolver asks a recursive resolver, often provided by an ISP or a public service such as Google or Cloudflare. That resolver does the walking.

The walk begins at a root server. The root does not know the address, but it knows which server handles the top-level domain. It sends the resolver to the server for `.com`, `.org`, or whatever the suffix is.

The top-level domain server does not know the address either, but it knows the authoritative server for the specific domain. It points the resolver there.

The authoritative server holds the zone file for the domain. It returns the record that maps the name to an IP address. The resolver hands that address back to the program.

Each answer carries a time-to-live value. The resolver caches it for that many seconds. A short TTL means the next lookup repeats the walk sooner; a long TTL saves time but keeps stale data longer.

If the name has a CNAME record, the resolver must look up the canonical name and start again. If the name has multiple A records, the resolver may return them in rotation.

The whole exchange usually takes milliseconds, but a slow or missing step can leave a page hanging.

A deadlock is a standoff between two or more threads, each holding a resource the other needs and waiting for the other to release it first.

Picture two narrow bridges over the same river. Car A is on the north bridge and wants the south bridge. Car B is on the south bridge and wants the north bridge. Both wait. Neither moves. Neither can back up.

In code, thread 1 locks account A and waits for account B. Thread 2 locks account B and waits for account A. Both hold a lock. Both need another. Both wait forever unless something breaks the cycle.

One way to avoid it is lock ordering. Every thread acquires locks in the same global order. If both threads always lock account A before account B, thread 2 cannot hold B while waiting for A. The circular wait becomes impossible because no thread can wait for a lock it should already hold.

Lock ordering works only when the order is simple and respected everywhere. When locks are scattered across modules or chosen at runtime, a single fixed order can be hard to enforce. Other defenses include timeouts, try-lock-and-back-off, and reducing the number of locks held at once.

A hash map stores each key-value pair in a bucket chosen by the key's hash code. When two keys land in the same bucket, that is a collision.

Most hash maps resolve collisions by chaining. Each bucket holds a linked list or tree of entries that share that bucket. A lookup hashes the key, walks the bucket's list, and compares keys until it finds a match.

Open addressing is the other common method. It stores every entry inside the table array itself. When a bucket is full, the probe sequence checks the next slot—linear, quadratic, or double hashing—until it finds the key or an empty slot.

Chaining keeps performance predictable as the table fills, at the cost of pointers and extra allocations. Open addressing uses less memory but degrades if the load factor climbs too high.

Resizing is the usual fix for too many collisions. The map creates a larger array, rehashes every entry into the new buckets, and the collision rate drops.
